# tracing - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tracing/^0.1/

## Expand description

A scoped, structured logging and diagnostics system.

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview

`tracing` is a framework for instrumenting Rust programs to collect
structured, event-based diagnostic information.

In asynchronous systems like Tokio, interpreting traditional log messages can
often be quite challenging. Since individual tasks are multiplexed on the same
thread, associated events and log lines are intermixed making it difficult to
trace the logic flow. `tracing` expands upon logging-style diagnostics by
allowing libraries and applications to record structured events with additional
information about *temporality* and *causality* — unlike a log message, a span
in `tracing` has a beginning and end time, may be entered and exited by the
flow of execution, and may exist within a nested tree of similar spans. In
addition, `tracing` spans are *structured*, with the ability to record typed
data as well as textual messages.

The `tracing` crate provides the APIs necessary for instrumenting libraries
and applications to emit trace data.

*Compiler support:  requires *

`rustc` 1.65+[§](https://docs.rs#core-concepts)Core Concepts

The core of `tracing`’s API is composed of *spans*, *events* and
*subscribers*. We’ll cover these in turn.

[§](https://docs.rs#spans)Spans

To record the flow of execution through a program, `tracing` introduces the
concept of [spans](https://docs.rs/span/index.html). Unlike a log line that represents a *moment in
time*, a span represents a *period of time* with a beginning and an end. When a
program begins executing in a context or performing a unit of work, it
*enters* that context’s span, and when it stops executing in that context,
it *exits* the span. The span in which a thread is currently executing is
referred to as that thread’s *current* span.

For example:

```
use tracing::{span, Level};
let span = span!(Level::TRACE, "my_span");
// `enter` returns a RAII guard which, when dropped, exits the span. this
// indicates that we are in the span for the current lexical scope.
let _enter = span.enter();
// perform some work in the context of `my_span`...
```
The [ span module](https://docs.rs/span/index.html)’s documentation provides further details on how to
use spans.

Warning: In asynchronous code that uses async/await syntax,`Span::enter`may produce incorrect traces if the returned drop guard is held across an await point. See[the method documentation](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html#in-asynchronous-code)for details.

[§](https://docs.rs#events)Events

An [ Event](https://docs.rs/struct.Event.html) represents a

*moment*in time. It signifies something that happened while a trace was being recorded.

`Event`s are comparable to the log
records emitted by unstructured logging code, but unlike a typical log line,
an `Event` may occur within the context of a span.For example:

```
use tracing::{event, span, Level};
// records an event outside of any span context:
event!(Level::INFO, "something happened");
let span = span!(Level::INFO, "my_span");
let _guard = span.enter();
// records an event within "my_span".
event!(Level::DEBUG, "something happened inside my_span");
```
In general, events should be used to represent points in time *within* a
span — a request returned with a given status code, *n* new items were
taken from a queue, and so on.

The [ Event struct](https://docs.rs/struct.Event.html) documentation provides further details on using
events.

[§](https://docs.rs#subscribers)Subscribers

As `Span`s and `Event`s occur, they are recorded or aggregated by
implementations of the [ Subscriber](https://docs.rs/trait.Subscriber.html) trait.

`Subscriber`s are notified
when an `Event` takes place and when a `Span` is entered or exited. These
notifications are represented by the following `Subscriber` trait methods:- `event`- `Event`takes place,
- `enter`- `Span`,
- `exit`- `Span`

In addition, subscribers may implement the [ enabled](https://docs.rs/trait.Subscriber.html#tymethod.enabled) function to

*filter*the notifications they receive based on

[metadata](https://docs.rs/struct.Metadata.html)describing each

`Span`
or `Event`. If a call to `Subscriber::enabled` returns `false` for a given
set of metadata, that `Subscriber` will *not*be notified about the corresponding

`Span` or `Event`. For performance reasons, if no currently
active subscribers express interest in a given set of metadata by returning
`true`, then the corresponding `Span` or `Event` will never be constructed.[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

First, add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies]
tracing = "0.1"
```
[§](https://docs.rs#recording-spans-and-events)Recording Spans and Events

Spans and events are recorded using macros.

[§](https://docs.rs#spans-1)Spans

The [ span!](https://docs.rs/macro.span.html) macro expands to a

[which is used to record a span. The](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html)

`Span` struct[method on that struct records that the span has been entered, and returns a](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html#method.enter)

`Span::enter`[RAII](https://github.com/rust-unofficial/patterns/blob/main/src/patterns/behavioural/RAII.md)guard object, which will exit the span when dropped.

For example:

```
use tracing::{span, Level};
// Construct a new span named "my span" with trace log level.
let span = span!(Level::TRACE, "my span");
// Enter the span, returning a guard object.
let _enter = span.enter();
// Any trace events that occur before the guard is dropped will occur
// within the span.
// Dropping the guard will exit the span.
```
The [ #[instrument]](https://docs.rs/tracing-attributes/latest/tracing_attributes/attr.instrument.html) attribute provides an easy way to
add

`tracing` spans to functions. A function annotated with `#[instrument]`
will create and enter a span with that function’s name every time the
function is called, with arguments to that function will be recorded as
fields using `fmt::Debug`.For example:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use tracing::{Level, event, instrument};
#[instrument]
pub fn my_function(my_arg: usize) {
    // This event will be recorded inside a span named `my_function` with the
    // field `my_arg`.
    event!(Level::INFO, "inside my_function!");
    // ...
}
```
For functions which don’t have built-in tracing support and can’t have
the `#[instrument]` attribute applied (such as from an external crate),
the [ Span struct](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html) has a

[which can be used to easily wrap synchronous code in a span.](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html#method.in_scope)

`in_scope()` methodFor example:

```
use tracing::info_span;
let json = info_span!("json.parse").in_scope(|| serde_json::from_slice(&buf))?;
```
You can find more examples showing how to use this crate [here](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tracing/tree/main/examples).

[§](https://docs.rs#events-1)Events

[ Event](https://docs.rs/struct.Event.html)s are recorded using the

[macro:](https://docs.rs/macro.event.html)

`event!````
use tracing::{event, Level};
event!(Level::INFO, "something has happened!");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#using-the-macros)Using the Macros

The [ span!](https://docs.rs/macro.span.html) and

[macros as well as the](https://docs.rs/macro.event.html)

`event!``#[instrument]` attribute
use fairly similar syntax, with some exceptions.[§](https://docs.rs#configuring-attributes)Configuring Attributes

Both macros require a [ Level](https://docs.rs/struct.Level.html) specifying the verbosity of the span or
event. Optionally, the,

[target](https://docs.rs/struct.Metadata.html#method.target)and

[parent span](https://docs.rs/span/struct.Attributes.html#method.parent)may be overridden. If the target and parent span are not overridden, they will default to the module path where the macro was invoked and the current span (as determined by the subscriber), respectively.

For example:

```
span!(target: "app_spans", Level::TRACE, "my span");
event!(target: "app_events", Level::INFO, "something has happened!");
```
```
let span = span!(Level::TRACE, "my span");
event!(parent: &span, Level::INFO, "something has happened!");
```
The span macros also take a string literal after the level, to set the name
of the span (as above).  In the case of the event macros, the name of the event can
be overridden (the default is `event file:line`) using the `name:` specifier.

```
span!(Level::TRACE, "my span");
event!(name: "some_info", Level::INFO, "something has happened!");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#recording-fields)Recording Fields

Structured fields on spans and events are specified using the syntax
`field_name = field_value`. Fields are separated by commas.

```
// records an event with two fields:
//  - "answer", with the value 42
//  - "question", with the value "life, the universe and everything"
event!(Level::INFO, answer = 42, question = "life, the universe, and everything");
```
As shorthand, local variables may be used as field values without an
assignment, similar to [struct initializers](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch05-01-defining-structs.html#using-the-field-init-shorthand-when-variables-and-fields-have-the-same-name). For example:

```
let user = "ferris";
span!(Level::TRACE, "login", user);
// is equivalent to:
span!(Level::TRACE, "login", user = user);
```
Field names can include dots, but should not be terminated by them:

```
let user = "ferris";
let email = "ferris@rust-lang.org";
span!(Level::TRACE, "login", user, user.email = email);
```
Since field names can include dots, fields on local structs can be used using the local variable shorthand:

```
let user = User {
    name: "ferris",
    email: "ferris@rust-lang.org",
};
// the span will have the fields `user.name = "ferris"` and
// `user.email = "ferris@rust-lang.org"`.
span!(Level::TRACE, "login", user.name, user.email);
```
Fields with names that are not Rust identifiers, or with names that are Rust reserved words, may be created using quoted string literals. However, this may not be used with the local variable shorthand.

```
// records an event with fields whose names are not Rust identifiers
//  - "guid:x-request-id", containing a `:`, with the value "abcdef"
//  - "type", which is a reserved word, with the value "request"
span!(Level::TRACE, "api", "guid:x-request-id" = "abcdef", "type" = "request");
```
Constant expressions can also be used as field names. Constants
must be enclosed in curly braces (`{}`) to indicate that the *value*
of the constant is to be used as the field name, rather than the
constant’s name. For example:

```
const RESOURCE_NAME: &str = "foo";
// this span will have the field `foo = "some_id"`
span!(Level::TRACE, "get", { RESOURCE_NAME } = "some_id");
```
The `?` sigil is shorthand that specifies a field should be recorded using
its [ fmt::Debug](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Debug.html) implementation:

```
#[derive(Debug)]
struct MyStruct {
    field: &'static str,
}
let my_struct = MyStruct {
    field: "Hello world!"
};
// `my_struct` will be recorded using its `fmt::Debug` implementation.
event!(Level::TRACE, greeting = ?my_struct);
// is equivalent to:
event!(Level::TRACE, greeting = tracing::field::debug(&my_struct));
```
The `%` sigil operates similarly, but indicates that the value should be
recorded using its [ fmt::Display](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html) implementation:

```
// `my_struct.field` will be recorded using its `fmt::Display` implementation.
event!(Level::TRACE, greeting = %my_struct.field);
// is equivalent to:
event!(Level::TRACE, greeting = tracing::field::display(&my_struct.field));
```
The `%` and `?` sigils may also be used with local variable shorthand:

```
// `my_struct.field` will be recorded using its `fmt::Display` implementation.
event!(Level::TRACE, %my_struct.field);
```
Additionally, a span may declare fields with the special value [ Empty](https://docs.rs/field/struct.Empty.html),
which indicates that that the value for that field does not currently exist
but may be recorded later. For example:

```
use tracing::{trace_span, field};
// Create a span with two fields: `greeting`, with the value "hello world", and
// `parting`, without a value.
let span = trace_span!("my_span", greeting = "hello world", parting = field::Empty);
// ...
// Now, record a value for parting as well.
span.record("parting", &"goodbye world!");
```
Finally, events may also include human-readable messages, in the form of a
[format string](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/fmt/index.html#usage) and (optional) arguments, **after** the event’s
key-value fields. If a format string and arguments are provided,
they will implicitly create a new field named `message` whose value is the
provided set of format arguments.

For example:

```
let question = "the ultimate question of life, the universe, and everything";
let answer = 42;
// records an event with the following fields:
// - `question.answer` with the value 42,
// - `question.tricky` with the value `true`,
// - "message", with the value "the answer to the ultimate question of life, the
//    universe, and everything is 42."
event!(
    Level::DEBUG,
    question.answer = answer,
    question.tricky = true,
    "the answer to {} is {}.", question, answer
);
```
Specifying a formatted message in this manner does not allocate by default.

[§](https://docs.rs#shorthand-macros)Shorthand Macros

`tracing` also offers a number of macros with preset verbosity levels.
The [ trace!](https://docs.rs/macro.trace.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/macro.debug.html)

`debug!`[,](https://docs.rs/macro.info.html)

`info!`[, and](https://docs.rs/macro.warn.html)

`warn!`[behave similarly to the](https://docs.rs/macro.error.html)

`error!`[macro, but with the](https://docs.rs/macro.event.html)

`event!`[argument already specified, while the corresponding](https://docs.rs/struct.Level.html)

`Level`[,](https://docs.rs/macro.trace_span.html)

`trace_span!`[,](https://docs.rs/macro.debug_span.html)

`debug_span!`[,](https://docs.rs/macro.info_span.html)

`info_span!`[, and](https://docs.rs/macro.warn_span.html)

`warn_span!`[macros are the same, but for the](https://docs.rs/macro.error_span.html)

`error_span!`[macro.](https://docs.rs/macro.span.html)

`span!`These are intended both as a shorthand, and for compatibility with the [ log](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.6/log/)
crate (see the next section).

[§](https://docs.rs#for-log-users)For `log` Users

Users of the [ log](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.6/log/) crate should note that

`tracing` exposes a set of
macros for creating `Event`s (`trace!`, `debug!`, `info!`, `warn!`, and
`error!`) which may be invoked with the same syntax as the similarly-named
macros from the `log` crate. Often, the process of converting a project to
use `tracing` can begin with a simple drop-in replacement.Let’s consider the `log` crate’s yak-shaving example:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use std::{error::Error, io};
use tracing::{debug, error, info, span, warn, Level};
// the `#[tracing::instrument]` attribute creates and enters a span
// every time the instrumented function is called. The span is named after the
// the function or method. Parameters passed to the function are recorded as fields.
#[tracing::instrument]
pub fn shave(yak: usize) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error + 'static>> {
    // this creates an event at the DEBUG level with two fields:
    // - `excitement`, with the key "excitement" and the value "yay!"
    // - `message`, with the key "message" and the value "hello! I'm gonna shave a yak."
    //
    // unlike other fields, `message`'s shorthand initialization is just the string itself.
    debug!(excitement = "yay!", "hello! I'm gonna shave a yak.");
    if yak == 3 {
        warn!("could not locate yak!");
        // note that this is intended to demonstrate `tracing`'s features, not idiomatic
        // error handling! in a library or application, you should consider returning
        // a dedicated `YakError`. libraries like snafu or thiserror make this easy.
        return Err(io::Error::new(io::ErrorKind::Other, "shaving yak failed!").into());
    } else {
        debug!("yak shaved successfully");
    }
    Ok(())
}
pub fn shave_all(yaks: usize) -> usize {
    // Constructs a new span named "shaving_yaks" at the TRACE level,
    // and a field whose key is "yaks". This is equivalent to writing:
    //
    // let span = span!(Level::TRACE, "shaving_yaks", yaks = yaks);
    //
    // local variables (`yaks`) can be used as field values
    // without an assignment, similar to struct initializers.
    let _span = span!(Level::TRACE, "shaving_yaks", yaks).entered();
    info!("shaving yaks");
    let mut yaks_shaved = 0;
    for yak in 1..=yaks {
        let res = shave(yak);
        debug!(yak, shaved = res.is_ok());
        if let Err(ref error) = res {
            // Like spans, events can also use the field initialization shorthand.
            // In this instance, `yak` is the field being initalized.
            error!(yak, error = error.as_ref(), "failed to shave yak!");
        } else {
            yaks_shaved += 1;
        }
        debug!(yaks_shaved);
    }
    yaks_shaved
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#in-libraries)In libraries

Libraries should link only to the `tracing` crate, and use the provided
macros to record whatever information will be useful to downstream
consumers.

[§](https://docs.rs#in-executables)In executables

In order to record trace events, executables have to use a `Subscriber`
implementation compatible with `tracing`. A `Subscriber` implements a
way of collecting trace data, such as by logging it to standard output.

This library does not contain any `Subscriber` implementations; these are
provided by [other crates](https://docs.rs#related-crates).

The simplest way to use a subscriber is to call the [ set_global_default](https://docs.rs/subscriber/fn.set_global_default.html)
function:

```
extern crate tracing;
let my_subscriber = FooSubscriber::new();
tracing::subscriber::set_global_default(my_subscriber)
    .expect("setting tracing default failed");
```
```

```
**Warning**: In general, libraries should *not* call
     `set_global_default()`! Doing so will cause conflicts when
     executables that depend on the library try to set the default later.

This subscriber will be used as the default in all threads for the
remainder of the duration of the program, similar to setting the logger
in the `log` crate.

In addition, the default subscriber can be set through using the
[ with_default](https://docs.rs/subscriber/fn.with_default.html) function. This follows the

`tokio` pattern of using
closures to represent executing code in a context that is exited at the end
of the closure. For example:```
let my_subscriber = FooSubscriber::new();
tracing::subscriber::with_default(my_subscriber, || {
    // Any trace events generated in this closure or by functions it calls
    // will be collected by `my_subscriber`.
})
```
This approach allows trace data to be collected by multiple subscribers within different contexts in the program. Note that the override only applies to the currently executing thread; other threads will not see the change from with_default.

Any trace events generated outside the context of a subscriber will not be collected.

Once a subscriber has been set, instrumentation points may be added to the
executable using the `tracing` crate’s macros.

[§](https://docs.rs#log-compatibility)`log` Compatibility

The [ log](https://docs.rs/log/0.4.6/log/) crate provides a simple, lightweight logging facade for Rust.
While

`tracing` builds upon `log`’s foundation with richer structured
diagnostic data, `log`’s simplicity and ubiquity make it the “lowest common
denominator” for text-based logging in Rust — a vast majority of Rust
libraries and applications either emit or consume `log` records. Therefore,
`tracing` provides multiple forms of interoperability with `log`: `tracing`
instrumentation can emit `log` records, and a compatibility layer enables
`tracing` [s to consume](https://docs.rs/trait.Subscriber.html)

`Subscriber``log` records as `tracing` [s.](https://docs.rs/struct.Event.html)

`Event`[§](https://docs.rs#emitting-log-records)Emitting `log` Records

This crate provides two feature flags, “log” and “log-always”, which will
cause [spans](https://docs.rs/span/index.html) and [events](https://docs.rs/struct.Event.html) to emit `log` records. When the “log” feature is
enabled, if no `tracing` `Subscriber` is active, invoking an event macro or
creating a span with fields will emit a `log` record. This is intended
primarily for use in libraries which wish to emit diagnostics that can be
consumed by applications using `tracing` *or* `log`, without paying the
additional overhead of emitting both forms of diagnostics when `tracing` is
in use.

Enabling the “log-always” feature will cause `log` records to be emitted
even if a `tracing` `Subscriber` *is* set. This is intended to be used in
applications where a `log` `Logger` is being used to record a textual log,
and `tracing` is used only to record other forms of diagnostics (such as
metrics, profiling, or distributed tracing data). Unlike the “log” feature,
libraries generally should **not** enable the “log-always” feature, as doing
so will prevent applications from being able to opt out of the `log` records.

See [here](https://docs.rs#crate-feature-flags) for more details on this crate’s feature flags.

The generated `log` records’ messages will be a string representation of the
span or event’s fields, and all additional information recorded by `log`
(target, verbosity level, module path, file, and line number) will also be
populated. Additionally, `log` records are also generated when spans are
entered, exited, and closed. Since these additional span lifecycle logs have
the potential to be very verbose, and don’t include additional fields, they
will always be emitted at the `Trace` level, rather than inheriting the
level of the span that generated them. Furthermore, they are categorized
under a separate `log` target, “tracing::span” (and its sub-target,
“tracing::span::active”, for the logs on entering and exiting a span), which
may be enabled or disabled separately from other `log` records emitted by
`tracing`.

[§](https://docs.rs#consuming-log-records)Consuming `log` Records

The [ tracing-log](https://crates.io/crates/tracing-log) crate provides a compatibility layer which
allows a

`tracing` [to consume](https://docs.rs/trait.Subscriber.html)

`Subscriber``log` records as though they
were `tracing` [events](https://docs.rs/struct.Event.html). This allows applications using

`tracing` to record
the logs emitted by dependencies using `log` as events within the context of
the application’s trace tree. See [that crate’s documentation](https://docs.rs/tracing-log/latest/tracing_log/#convert-log-records-to-tracing-events)for details.

[§](https://docs.rs#related-crates)Related Crates

In addition to `tracing` and `tracing-core`, the [ tokio-rs/tracing](https://github.com/tokio-rs/tracing) repository
contains several additional crates designed to be used with the

`tracing` ecosystem.
This includes a collection of `Subscriber` implementations, as well as utility
and adapter crates to assist in writing `Subscriber`s and instrumenting
applications.In particular, the following crates are likely to be of interest:

- `tracing-futures`- `futures`crate, allowing spans to be attached to- `Future`s,- `Stream`s, and- `Executor`s.
- `tracing-subscriber`- `Subscriber`implementations and utilities for working with- `Subscriber`s. This includes a- `FmtSubscriber`- `FmtSubscriber`for logging formatted trace data to stdout, with similar filtering and formatting to the- `env_logger`
- `tracing-log`- `log`- `tracing`- `Event`s within the trace tree. This is useful when a project using- `tracing`have dependencies which use- `log`. Note that if you’re using- `tracing-subscriber`’s- `FmtSubscriber`, you don’t need to depend on- `tracing-log`directly.
- `tracing-appender`

maintained by the `tokio` project. These include:

- `tracing-wasm`- `Subscriber`/- `Layer`implementation that reports events and spans via browser- `console.log`and- [User Timing API (](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/User_Timing_API).- `window.performance`)
- `tracing-web`- `console.*`and span events to the- [User Timing API (](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/User_Timing_API).- `window.performance`)
- `tide-tracing`- [tide](https://crates.io/crates/tide)middleware to trace all incoming requests and responses.

- `tracing-logfmt`

If you’re the maintainer of a `tracing` ecosystem crate not listed above,
please let us know! We’d love to add your project to the list!

```

```
**Note**: Some of these ecosystem crates are currently
     unreleased and/or in earlier stages of development. They may be less stable

[§](https://docs.rs#crate-feature-flags)Crate Feature Flags

The following crate [feature flags](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html#the-features-section) are available:

-
A set of features controlling the [static verbosity level](https://docs.rs/level_filters/index.html#compile-time-filters).
-
`log`: causes trace instrumentation points to emit`log``tracing`subscriber has not been set. This is intended for use in libraries whose users may be using either`tracing`or`log`.
-
`log-always`: Emit`log`records from all`tracing`spans and events, even if a`tracing`subscriber has been set. This should be set only by applications which intend to collect traces and logs separately; if an adapter is used to convert`log`records into`tracing`events, this will cause duplicate events to occur.
-
`attributes`: Includes support for the`#[instrument]`attribute. This is on by default, but does bring in the`syn`crate as a dependency, which may add to the compile time of crates that do not already use it.
-
`std`: Depend on the Rust standard library (enabled by default).`no_std`users may disable this feature with`default-features = false`:`[dependencies] tracing = { version = "0.1.38", default-features = false }`

```

```
**Note**: `tracing`'s `no_std` support
     requires `liballoc`.

[§](https://docs.rs#unstable-features)Unstable Features

These feature flags enable **unstable** features. The public API may break in 0.1.x
releases. To enable these features, the `--cfg tracing_unstable` must be passed to
`rustc` when compiling.

The following unstable feature flags are currently available:

- `valuable`: Enables support for recording- [field values](https://docs.rs/field/index.html)using the- `valuable`

[§](https://docs.rs#enabling-unstable-features)Enabling Unstable Features

The easiest way to set the `tracing_unstable` cfg is to use the `RUSTFLAGS`
env variable when running `cargo` commands:

`RUSTFLAGS="--cfg tracing_unstable" cargo build`Alternatively, the following can be added to the `.cargo/config` file in a
project to automatically enable the cfg flag for that project:

```
[build]
rustflags = ["--cfg", "tracing_unstable"]
```
[§](https://docs.rs#supported-rust-versions)Supported Rust Versions

Tracing is built against the latest stable release. The minimum supported version is 1.65. The current Tracing version is not guaranteed to build on Rust versions earlier than the minimum supported version.

Tracing follows the same compiler support policies as the rest of the Tokio project. The current stable Rust compiler and the three most recent minor versions before it will always be supported. For example, if the current stable compiler version is 1.69, the minimum supported version will not be increased past 1.66, three minor versions prior. Increasing the minimum supported compiler version is not considered a semver breaking change as long as doing so complies with this policy.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [dispatcher](https://docs.rs/dispatcher/index.html)
- Dispatches trace events to `Subscriber`
- [event](https://docs.rs/event/index.html)
- Events represent single points in time during the execution of a program.
- [field](https://docs.rs/field/index.html)
- `Span`and- `Event`key-value data.
- [instrument](https://docs.rs/instrument/index.html)
- Attach a span to a `std::future::Future`.
- [level_](https://docs.rs/level_filters/index.html)- filters
- Trace verbosity level filtering.
- [span](https://docs.rs/span/index.html)
- Spans represent periods of time in which a program was executing in a particular context.
- [subscriber](https://docs.rs/subscriber/index.html)
- Collects and records trace data.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [debug](https://docs.rs/macro.debug.html)
- Constructs an event at the debug level.
- [debug_](https://docs.rs/macro.debug_span.html)- span
- Constructs a span at the debug level.
- [enabled](https://docs.rs/macro.enabled.html)
- Checks whether a span or event is [enabled](https://docs.rs/trait.Subscriber.html#tymethod.enabled)based on the provided[metadata](https://docs.rs/struct.Metadata.html).
- [error](https://docs.rs/macro.error.html)
- Constructs an event at the error level.
- [error_](https://docs.rs/macro.error_span.html)- span
- Constructs a span at the error level.
- [event](https://docs.rs/macro.event.html)
- Constructs a new `Event`.
- [event_](https://docs.rs/macro.event_enabled.html)- enabled
- Tests whether an event with the specified level and target would be enabled.
- [info](https://docs.rs/macro.info.html)
- Constructs an event at the info level.
- [info_](https://docs.rs/macro.info_span.html)- span
- Constructs a span at the info level.
- [record_](https://docs.rs/macro.record_all.html)- all
- Records multiple values on a span in a single call. As with recording individual values, all fields must be declared when the span is created.
- [span](https://docs.rs/macro.span.html)
- Constructs a new span.
- [span_](https://docs.rs/macro.span_enabled.html)- enabled
- Tests whether a span with the specified level and target would be enabled.
- [trace](https://docs.rs/macro.trace.html)
- Constructs an event at the trace level.
- [trace_](https://docs.rs/macro.trace_span.html)- span
- Constructs a span at the trace level.
- [warn](https://docs.rs/macro.warn.html)
- Constructs an event at the warn level.
- [warn_](https://docs.rs/macro.warn_span.html)- span
- Constructs a span at the warn level.

- [Dispatch](https://docs.rs/struct.Dispatch.html)
- `Dispatch`trace data to a- `Subscriber`
- [Event](https://docs.rs/struct.Event.html)
- `Event`s represent single points in time where something occurred during the execution of a program.
- [Level](https://docs.rs/struct.Level.html)
- Describes the level of verbosity of a span or event.
- [Metadata](https://docs.rs/struct.Metadata.html)
- Metadata describing a [span](https://docs.rs/tracing-core/0.1.36/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/tracing_core/span/index.html)or[event](https://docs.rs/event/index.html).
- [Span](https://docs.rs/struct.Span.html)
- A handle representing a span, with the capability to enter the span if it exists.

- [Instrument](https://docs.rs/trait.Instrument.html)
- Attaches spans to a `std::future::Future`
- [Subscriber](https://docs.rs/trait.Subscriber.html)
- Trait representing the functions required to collect trace data.

- A field value of an erased type.

- Instruments a function to create and enter a `tracing`[span](https://docs.rs/tracing/latest/tracing/span/index.html)every time the function is called.

# ulid - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ulid/^1.2/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#ulid-rs)ulid-rs

This is a Rust implementation of the [ulid](https://github.com/ulid/spec) project which provides
Universally Unique Lexicographically Sortable Identifiers.

[§](https://docs.rs#quickstart)Quickstart

```
// Generate a ulid
let ulid = Ulid::new();
// Generate a string for a ulid
let s = ulid.to_string();
// Create from a String
let res = Ulid::from_string(&s);
assert_eq!(ulid, res.unwrap());
// Or using FromStr
let res = s.parse();
assert_eq!(ulid, res.unwrap());
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [serde](https://docs.rs/serde/index.html)
- Serialization and deserialization.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Archived](https://docs.rs/struct.ArchivedUlid.html)- Ulid
- An archived `Ulid`
- [Generator](https://docs.rs/struct.Generator.html)
- A Ulid generator that provides monotonically increasing Ulids
- [Ulid](https://docs.rs/struct.Ulid.html)
- A Ulid is a unique 128-bit lexicographically sortable identifier
- [Ulid](https://docs.rs/struct.UlidResolver.html)- Resolver
- The resolver for an archived `Ulid`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Decode](https://docs.rs/enum.DecodeError.html)- Error
- An error that can occur when decoding a base32 string
- [Encode](https://docs.rs/enum.EncodeError.html)- Error
- An error that can occur when encoding a base32 string
- [Monotonic](https://docs.rs/enum.MonotonicError.html)- Error
- Error while trying to generate a monotonic increment in the same millisecond

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [ULID_](https://docs.rs/constant.ULID_LEN.html)- LEN
- Length of a string-encoded Ulid

# criterion - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/criterion/^0.8/

## Expand description

A statistics-driven micro-benchmarking library written in Rust.

This crate is a microbenchmarking library which aims to provide strong statistical confidence in detecting and estimating the size of performance improvements and regressions, while also being easy to use.

See
[the user guide](https://criterion-rs.github.io/book/index.html)
for examples as well as details on the measurement and analysis process,
and the output.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features:

- Collects detailed statistics, providing strong confidence that changes to performance are real, not measurement noise.
- Produces detailed charts, providing thorough understanding of your code’s performance behavior.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [async_](https://docs.rs/async_executor/index.html)- executor
- This module defines a trait that can be used to plug in different Futures executors into Criterion.rs’ async benchmarking support.
- [measurement](https://docs.rs/measurement/index.html)
- This module defines a set of traits that can be used to plug different measurements (eg.
Unix’s Processor Time, CPU or GPU performance counters, etc.) into Criterion.rs. It also
includes the `WallTime`
- [profiler](https://docs.rs/profiler/index.html)
- This module provides an extension trait which allows in-process profilers
to be hooked into the `--profile-time`argument at compile-time. Users of out-of-process profilers such as perf don’t need to do anything special.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [criterion_](https://docs.rs/macro.criterion_group.html)- group
- Macro used to define a function group for the benchmark harness; see the
`criterion_main!`
- [criterion_](https://docs.rs/macro.criterion_main.html)- main
- Macro which expands to a benchmark harness.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Async](https://docs.rs/struct.AsyncBencher.html)- Bencher
- Async/await variant of `Bencher`
- [Bencher](https://docs.rs/struct.Bencher.html)
- Timer struct used to iterate a benchmarked function and measure the runtime.
- [Benchmark](https://docs.rs/struct.BenchmarkGroup.html)- Group
- Structure used to group together a set of related benchmarks, along with custom configuration settings for groups of benchmarks. All benchmarks performed using a benchmark group will be grouped together in the final report.
- [Benchmark](https://docs.rs/struct.BenchmarkId.html)- Id
- Simple structure representing an ID for a benchmark. The ID must be unique within a benchmark group.
- [Criterion](https://docs.rs/struct.Criterion.html)
- The benchmark manager
- [Plot](https://docs.rs/struct.PlotConfiguration.html)- Configuration
- Contains the configuration options for the plots generated by a particular benchmark or benchmark group.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Axis](https://docs.rs/enum.AxisScale.html)- Scale
- Axis scaling type. Specified via `PlotConfiguration::summary_scale`
- [Baseline](https://docs.rs/enum.Baseline.html)
- Baseline describes how the `baseline_directory`is handled.
- [Batch](https://docs.rs/enum.BatchSize.html)- Size
- Argument to `Bencher::iter_batched``Bencher::iter_batched_ref`
- [Benchmark](https://docs.rs/enum.BenchmarkFilter.html)- Filter
- Benchmark filtering support.
- [Plotting](https://docs.rs/enum.PlottingBackend.html)- Backend
- Enum used to select the plotting backend.
- [Sampling](https://docs.rs/enum.SamplingMode.html)- Mode
- This enum allows the user to control how Criterion.rs chooses the iteration count when sampling.
The default is `Auto`, which will choose a method automatically based on the iteration time during the warm-up phase.
- [Throughput](https://docs.rs/enum.Throughput.html)
- Enum representing different ways of measuring the throughput of benchmarked code. If the throughput setting is configured for a benchmark then the estimated throughput will be reported as well as the time per iteration.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [black_](https://docs.rs/fn.black_box.html)- box - Deprecated
- A function that is opaque to the optimizer, used to prevent the compiler from optimizing away computations in a benchmark.

# rand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand/^0.10/

## Expand description

Random-number generators and samplers

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

```
// rand::random() supports many common types:
println!("Uniform i8 sample: {}", match rand::random() {
    0i8 => "zero",
    i if i > 0 => "positive",
    _ => "negative",
});
// Ranged sampling:
use std::f32::consts::PI;
println!("Angle: {} degrees", rand::random_range(-PI..PI));
```
See also [The Book: Quick Start](https://rust-random.github.io/book/quick-start.html).

# rcgen - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rcgen/^0.14/

## Expand description

Rust X.509 certificate generation utility

This crate provides a way to generate self signed X.509 certificates.

The most simple way of using this crate is by calling the
[ generate_simple_self_signed](https://docs.rs/fn.generate_simple_self_signed.html) function.
For more customization abilities, construct a

[and a key pair to call](https://docs.rs/struct.CertificateParams.html)

`CertificateParams`[or](https://docs.rs/struct.CertificateParams.html#method.signed_by)

`CertificateParams::signed_by()`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.CertificateParams.html#method.self_signed)

`CertificateParams::self_signed()`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rcgen::{generate_simple_self_signed, CertifiedKey};
// Generate a certificate that's valid for "localhost" and "hello.world.example"
let subject_alt_names = vec!["hello.world.example".to_string(),
	"localhost".to_string()];
let CertifiedKey { cert, signing_key } = generate_simple_self_signed(subject_alt_names).unwrap();
println!("{}", cert.pem());
println!("{}", signing_key.serialize_pem());
```

# tempfile - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tempfile/^3.27/

## Expand description

This is a library for creating temporary files and directories that are automatically deleted when no longer referenced (i.e., on drop).

- Use `tempfile()``std::fs::File`
- Use `NamedTempFile::new()`*named*temporary file that can be referred to its path.
- Use `tempdir()`
- Use `spooled_tempfile()`

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

This crate provides several approaches to creating temporary files and directories.
[ tempfile()](https://docs.rs/fn.tempfile.html) relies on the OS to remove the temporary file once the last handle is closed.

[and](https://docs.rs/struct.TempDir.html)

`TempDir`[both rely on Rust destructors for cleanup.](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html)

`NamedTempFile`[§](https://docs.rs#resource-leaking)Resource Leaking

`tempfile` will (almost) never fail to cleanup temporary resources. However `TempDir` and
`NamedTempFile` will fail if their destructors don’t run. This is because `tempfile` relies on
the OS to cleanup the underlying file, while `TempDir` and `NamedTempFile` rely on rust
destructors to do so. Destructors may fail to run if the process exits through an unhandled
signal interrupt (like `SIGINT`), or if the instance is declared statically (like with
[ lazy_static](https://github.com/rust-lang-nursery/lazy-static.rs/issues/62)), among other possible reasons.

[§](https://docs.rs#unexpected-file-deletion)Unexpected File Deletion

Most operating systems periodically clean up temporary files that haven’t been accessed recently
(often on the order of multiple days). This issue does not affect unnamed temporary files but
can invalidate the paths associated with named temporary files on Unix-like systems because the
temporary file can be unlinked from the filesystem while still open and in-use. See the
[temporary file cleaner](https://docs.rs#temporary-file-cleaners) section for more security implications.

[§](https://docs.rs#security)Security

This section discusses security issues relevant to Unix-like operating systems that use shared temporary directories by default. Importantly, it’s not relevant for Windows or macOS as both operating systems use private per-user temporary directories by default.

Applications can mitigate the issues described below by using [ env::override_temp_dir](https://docs.rs/env/fn.override_temp_dir.html) to
change the default temporary directory but should do so if and only if default the temporary
directory (

[) is unsuitable (is world readable, world writable, managed by a temporary file cleaner, etc.).](https://docs.rs/env/fn.temp_dir.html)

`env::temp_dir`[§](https://docs.rs#temporary-file-cleaners)Temporary File Cleaners

In the presence of pathological temporary file cleaner, relying on file paths is unsafe because a temporary file cleaner could delete the temporary file which an attacker could then replace.

This isn’t an issue for [ tempfile](https://docs.rs/fn.tempfile.html) as it doesn’t rely on file paths. However,

[and temporary directories](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html)

`NamedTempFile`*do*rely on file paths for

*some*operations. See the security documentation on the

[and the](https://docs.rs/struct.NamedTempFile.html)

`NamedTempFile`[types for more information.](https://docs.rs/struct.TempDir.html)

`TempDir`Mitigation:

- This is rarely an issue for short-lived files as temporary file cleaners usually only remove temporary files that haven’t been modified or accessed within many (10-30) days.
- Very long lived temporary files should be placed in directories not managed by temporary file cleaners.

[§](https://docs.rs#access-permissions)Access Permissions

Temporary *files* created with this library are private by default on all operating systems.
However, temporary *directories* are created with the default permissions and will therefore be
world-readable by default unless the user has changed their umask and/or default temporary
directory.

[§](https://docs.rs#denial-of-service)Denial of Service

If the file-name randomness ([ Builder::rand_bytes](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.rand_bytes)) is too small and/or this crate is built
without the

`getrandom` feature, it may be possible for an attacker to predict the random file
names chosen by this library, preventing temporary file creation by creating temporary files
with these predicted file names. By default, this library mitigates this denial of service
attack by:- Defaulting to 6 random characters per temporary file forcing an attacker to create billions of files before random collisions are expected (at which point you probably have larger problems).
- Re-seeding the random filename generator from system randomness after 3 failed attempts to
create temporary a file (when the `getrandom`feature is enabled as it is by default on all major platforms).

[§](https://docs.rs#early-drop-pitfall)Early drop pitfall

Because `TempDir` and `NamedTempFile` rely on their destructors for cleanup, this can lead
to an unexpected early removal of the directory/file, usually when working with APIs which are
generic over `AsRef<Path>`. Consider the following example:

```
use tempfile::tempdir;
use std::process::Command;
// Create a directory inside of `env::temp_dir()`.
let temp_dir = tempdir()?;
// Spawn the `touch` command inside the temporary directory and collect the exit status
// Note that `temp_dir` is **not** moved into `current_dir`, but passed as a reference
let exit_status = Command::new("touch").arg("tmp").current_dir(&temp_dir).status()?;
assert!(exit_status.success());
```
This works because a reference to `temp_dir` is passed to `current_dir`, resulting in the
destructor of `temp_dir` being run after the `Command` has finished execution. Moving the
`TempDir` into the `current_dir` call would result in the `TempDir` being converted into
an internal representation, with the original value being dropped and the directory thus
being deleted, before the command can be executed.

The `touch` command would fail with an `No such file or directory` error.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Create a temporary file and write some data into it:

```
use tempfile::tempfile;
use std::io::Write;
// Create a file inside of `env::temp_dir()`.
let mut file = tempfile()?;
writeln!(file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
```
Create a named temporary file and open an independent file handle:

```
use tempfile::NamedTempFile;
use std::io::{Write, Read};
let text = "Brian was here. Briefly.";
// Create a file inside of `env::temp_dir()`.
let mut file1 = NamedTempFile::new()?;
// Re-open it.
let mut file2 = file1.reopen()?;
// Write some test data to the first handle.
file1.write_all(text.as_bytes())?;
// Read the test data using the second handle.
let mut buf = String::new();
file2.read_to_string(&mut buf)?;
assert_eq!(buf, text);
```
Create a temporary directory and add a file to it:

```
use tempfile::tempdir;
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::Write;
// Create a directory inside of `env::temp_dir()`.
let dir = tempdir()?;
let file_path = dir.path().join("my-temporary-note.txt");
let mut file = File::create(file_path)?;
writeln!(file, "Brian was here. Briefly.")?;
// By closing the `TempDir` explicitly, we can check that it has
// been deleted successfully. If we don't close it explicitly,
// the directory will still be deleted when `dir` goes out
// of scope, but we won't know whether deleting the directory
// succeeded.
drop(file);
dir.close()?;
```

# evento_accord - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/evento-accord/2.0.0-alpha.24/target-redirect/evento_accord/

## Expand description

Accord consensus protocol (Apache Cassandra [CEP-15](https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/display/CASSANDRA/CEP-15:+General+Purpose+Transactions)) for evento.

This crate is building toward a new evento [ Executor](https://docs.rs/evento-core/2.0.0-alpha.24/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/evento_core/executor/trait.Executor.html) that turns evento
into a

**leaderless, strictly-serializable, highly-available replicated event store**: events are replicated across

`N = 2f + 1` nodes with a single
global serial order and no elected leader, tolerating `f` failures.See `DESIGN.md` for the full architecture and milestone plan. The crate is
currently at **M0 (skeleton)**: the [ api](https://docs.rs/api/index.html) traits, core types, an in-memory
transport, and a tested Hybrid Logical Clock are in place; the protocol
phases (M1+) are not yet implemented.

[§](https://docs.rs#layering)Layering

```
Executor impl (M5) → Coordinator → protocol core → api traits
                                                    (MessageSink, Topology,
                                                     Clock, Journal, DataStore)
```
The protocol depends only on the [ api](https://docs.rs/api/index.html) traits, each with a deterministic
in-process implementation for testing and a production implementation.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [api](https://docs.rs/api/index.html)
- Host-facing trait interfaces, modelled on `accord-core`’s`accord/api`package. The protocol core depends only on these traits; each has a deterministic in-process implementation for the simulation harness and a production implementation (real transport, static-config membership, Fjall/SQL-backed storage).
- [clock](https://docs.rs/clock/index.html)
- Cluster node identity and the Hybrid Logical Clock.
- [executor](https://docs.rs/executor/index.html)
- Wiring Accord into evento’s `Executor`
- [failure_](https://docs.rs/failure_detector/index.html)- detector
- Phi-accrual failure detector (Hayashibara et al.).
- [format](https://docs.rs/format/index.html)
- On-the-wire and on-disk record framing: a small, explicit version tag in front of every bitcode payload, so a format change is detectable instead of silently mis-parsed.
- [message](https://docs.rs/message/index.html)
- Wire messages and per-transaction command state.
- [metrics](https://docs.rs/metrics/index.html)
- Lightweight runtime counters for observability.
- [node](https://docs.rs/node/index.html)
- A cluster node: one replica plus the coordinator logic for client writes and for recovering transactions whose coordinator has failed.
- [replica](https://docs.rs/replica/index.html)
- Replica-side consensus state machine.
- [store](https://docs.rs/store/index.html)
- In-memory `DataStore``Journal`
- [tcp](https://docs.rs/tcp/index.html)
- Production transport: length-delimited framed TCP behind the
`MessageSink`
- [transport](https://docs.rs/transport/index.html)
- In-memory `MessageSink`

# evento_accord::api - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/evento-accord/2.0.0-alpha.24/evento_accord/api/index.html

## Expand description

Host-facing trait interfaces, modelled on `accord-core`’s `accord/api`
package. The protocol core depends only on these traits; each has a
deterministic in-process implementation for the simulation harness and a
production implementation (real transport, static-config membership,
Fjall/SQL-backed storage).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Acceptor](https://docs.rs/struct.AcceptorRecord.html)- Record
- A config-Paxos acceptor’s durable state for one epoch — the highest ballot it
has promised and the highest-ballot layout it has accepted, if any. Persisted
(via `Journal::record_acceptor`**before**the matching promise/accept reply is sent, so a restarted acceptor restores its`promised`ballot and can never regress to a lower one (the Paxos crash-safety requirement).
- [Dynamic](https://docs.rs/struct.DynamicTopology.html)- Topology
- A `Topology`**epoch**.
- [Sharded](https://docs.rs/struct.ShardedTopology.html)- Topology
- Range-/hash-partitioned `Topology`**disjoint**shards: the key space is split across shards, each owned by its own replica set, and every node belongs to exactly one shard. A transaction touching keys in several shards must reach a quorum in each. Used for M3 multi-shard transactions.
- [Static](https://docs.rs/struct.StaticTopology.html)- Topology
- Static, single-shard `Topology`

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Data](https://docs.rs/trait.DataStore.html)- Store
- Applied state — the materialised event store on a replica. Backed by an
existing evento backend (`Fjall`/`Sql`). This is where committed transactions land in execution-timestamp order and where reads, subscriptions, and snapshots are served.
- [Journal](https://docs.rs/trait.Journal.html)
- Durable command log. Each replica persists its `CommandState`
- [Message](https://docs.rs/trait.MessageSink.html)- Sink
- Outbound transport. The protocol core sends a `Message``NodeId``TxnId`inside the message, not by the transport. Implementations: in-memory channels (tests) and length-delimited framed TCP (production).
- [Topology](https://docs.rs/trait.Topology.html)
- Cluster membership and key→replica-set mapping for the current epoch.

---

             'life0: 'async_trait { ... }
}## Expand description

Applied state — the materialised event store on a replica. Backed by an
existing evento backend (`Fjall` / `Sql`). This is where committed
transactions land in execution-timestamp order and where reads,
subscriptions, and snapshots are served.

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/api.rs.html#230)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/api.rs.html#230)

Current version of an aggregate. Returns 0 for an aggregate with no events. Used during the Read phase to evaluate the optimistic-version condition before any shard appends.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/api.rs.html#237-243)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/api.rs.html#237-243)

Records a decided transaction at its execution timestamp. When
`commit` is true the `events` are appended (advancing versions);
otherwise the transaction is a no-op (an aborted conditional write).
Implementations must apply in `execute_at` order to preserve the global
serial order. `events` is only this replica’s owned subset.

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

    Self: 'async_trait,
    'life0: 'async_trait,

Serves a read query from the local backend, so a node can answer reads forwarded to it for a key range it owns. The default returns nothing (a store that holds no queryable events, e.g. the in-memory test store).

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/api.rs.html#261-263)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/api.rs.html#261-263)

All applied events materialised in this store — the bootstrap snapshot a joining node installs to reconstruct the state that log truncation has removed from the command journal. The default is empty (a store whose journal never truncates needs no snapshot).

## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait **is** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# DynamicTopology in evento_accord::api - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/evento-accord/2.0.0-alpha.24/evento_accord/api/struct.DynamicTopology.html

`pub struct DynamicTopology { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A [ Topology](https://docs.rs/trait.Topology.html) whose shard layout can be replaced atomically as the cluster
grows. Each layout is tagged with a monotonically increasing

**epoch**.

Unlike [ ShardedTopology](https://docs.rs/struct.ShardedTopology.html), the running node need not yet belong to any shard
(a joining node holds the current layout to find a peer to bootstrap from,
then

[s the new epoch that includes it). Coordinating the epoch change across the cluster — and handling transactions in flight across it — is future work; callers install an agreed layout.](https://docs.rs/struct.DynamicTopology.html#method.install)

`install`## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Builds a topology at `epoch` from disjoint shard replica sets. `this` need
not be a member yet.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/api.rs.html#519-522)#### pub fn [with_regions](https://docs.rs#method.with_regions)(self, regions: [HashMap](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/hash/map/struct.HashMap.html)<[NodeId](https://docs.rs/clock/struct.NodeId.html), [RegionId](https://docs.rs/type.RegionId.html)>) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/api.rs.html#519-522)

#### pub fn [with_regions](https://docs.rs#method.with_regions)(self, regions: [HashMap](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/hash/map/struct.HashMap.html)<[NodeId](https://docs.rs/clock/struct.NodeId.html), [RegionId](https://docs.rs/type.RegionId.html)>) -> Self

Tags nodes with regions, enabling region-aware read routing and the
**region-derived fast-path electorate** (a node absent from the map has no
region). The map must be identical on every node.

## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/api.rs.html#576-656)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Topology-for-DynamicTopology)

### impl [Topology](https://docs.rs/trait.Topology.html) for [DynamicTopology](https://docs.rs/struct.DynamicTopology.html)

The **region-derived** electorate for `key`’s shard (see
[ electorate_for](https://docs.rs/struct.DynamicTopology.html#method.electorate_for)). A pure function of the
installed layout + region tags, so it is recomputed correctly after every
epoch change with no extra state crossing consensus.

Atomically replaces the layout with a later `epoch`. Ignored if `epoch`
is not newer than the current one.

`key` — the set a transaction touching `key` must reach
quorum within.[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/api.rs.html#619-623)[§](https://docs.rs#method.slow_quorum)#### fn [slow_quorum](https://docs.rs/trait.Topology.html#tymethod.slow_quorum)(&self, key: &[Key](https://docs.rs/message/struct.Key.html)) -> [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)

`key`’s replica set: `f + 1`.`key`. Single-shard topologies return `0`.`node` replicates, if any. Shards are disjoint, so a node
belongs to at most one. Single-shard topologies return `Some(0)`.`node` lives in, if regions are configured. Used to

             'life0: 'async_trait { ... }
}## Expand description

Durable command log. Each replica persists its [ CommandState](https://docs.rs/message/struct.CommandState.html) per
transaction so it survives restarts and can be replayed during recovery.

Two write paths support **group commit**: [ stage](https://docs.rs/trait.Journal.html#method.stage) buffers a
write that must be durable no later than the next

[, and](https://docs.rs/trait.Journal.html#method.flush)

`flush``flush` makes every staged write durable in one fsync. The node’s inbox
loop drains a batch of messages, stages each, then flushes once — amortizing
the fsync across the batch. [is the immediate (stage-then-flush) path for callers that need durability right away.](https://docs.rs/trait.Journal.html#tymethod.record)

`record`## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/api.rs.html#170-173)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/api.rs.html#170-173)

Discards every record whose transaction is below `before` (its
transactions are redundant — applied on every replica) and persists
`before` as the truncation watermark, so a restart sets its redundancy
floor and trusts the data store for everything below it. Bounds the log to
in-flight work. The default is a no-op (a non-truncating journal).

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/api.rs.html#177-179)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/api.rs.html#177-179)

The persisted truncation watermark, if any — the redundancy floor a restart restores. The default returns nothing.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/api.rs.html#186-188)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/api.rs.html#186-188)

All persisted command states, for rebuilding replica state after a process restart. The default returns nothing (a non-durable journal).

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/api.rs.html#194-197)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/api.rs.html#194-197)

Durably appends a decided metadata-log entry — one `epoch`’s committed
topology `layout`. Durable by the time it returns. Idempotent: re-appending
an epoch already present with the same layout is a no-op. The default is a
no-op (a journal that does not back dynamic membership).

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/api.rs.html#201-203)

All persisted metadata-log entries, ascending by epoch, for replaying the committed topology sequence after a restart. The default returns nothing.

# RegionId in evento_accord::api - Rust

`pub type RegionId = `[u16](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u16.html);## Expand description

Identifies a region / datacenter — a locality group of nodes. Used to prefer same-region peers for lower-latency operations (e.g. read routing).

# ShardedTopology in evento_accord::api - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/evento-accord/2.0.0-alpha.24/evento_accord/api/struct.ShardedTopology.html

`pub struct ShardedTopology { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Range-/hash-partitioned [ Topology](https://docs.rs/trait.Topology.html) with

**disjoint**shards: the key space is split across shards, each owned by its own replica set, and every node belongs to exactly one shard. A transaction touching keys in several shards must reach a quorum in each. Used for M3 multi-shard transactions.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Builds a topology from disjoint shard replica sets and this node’s id.

Panics if `this` is not in any shard, or if the shards are not disjoint.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/api.rs.html#412-415)

Sets `shard`’s fast-path electorate — the subset of its replicas whose
`PreAccept` votes decide the one-round-trip fast path (see
[ Topology::fast_electorate](https://docs.rs/trait.Topology.html#method.fast_electorate)). Panics unless it is a subset of the shard’s
replicas with

`f + 1 ≤ |E| ≤ N`.## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

### impl [Topology](https://docs.rs/trait.Topology.html) for [ShardedTopology](https://docs.rs/struct.ShardedTopology.html)

`key` — the set a transaction touching `key` must reach
quorum within.**fast-path electorate**for

`key`’s shard — the subset of
[whose](https://docs.rs/trait.Topology.html#tymethod.replicas)

`replicas``PreAccept` votes decide the
one-round-trip fast path. It is a *fixed, cluster-agreed*property of the shard (every coordinator of the shard uses the same set), placed in one region so a co-located coordinator commits in a single local round-trip.

`key`’s replica set: `f + 1`.`key`. Single-shard topologies return `0`.`node` replicates, if any. Shards are disjoint, so a node
belongs to at most one. Single-shard topologies return `Some(0)`.`node` lives in, if regions are configured. Used to
prefer a same-region peer (e.g. for read routing). The default is `None`
(no region awareness — all nodes treated as one locality).`node` replicates `key` (i.e. owns its shard). Determines which
events of a multi-shard transaction a replica reads and applies.`false` (fixed topologies); [overrides it to](https://docs.rs/struct.DynamicTopology.html)

`DynamicTopology``true`. The
node’s metadata-log catch-up sweep only runs for dynamic topologies, so a
fixed-membership cluster issues no control-plane traffic.## Auto Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#synthetic-implementations)

}## Expand description

Cluster membership and key→replica-set mapping for the current epoch.

Implementations: [ StaticTopology](https://docs.rs/struct.StaticTopology.html) (a fixed node list, single shard) and

[(disjoint, hash-partitioned shards). Epochs and dynamic membership arrive in M4.](https://docs.rs/struct.ShardedTopology.html)

`ShardedTopology`## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

Replicas that own `key` — the set a transaction touching `key` must reach
quorum within.

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/api.rs.html#72-74)#### fn [fast_electorate](https://docs.rs#method.fast_electorate)(&self, key: &[Key](https://docs.rs/message/struct.Key.html)) -> [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[NodeId](https://docs.rs/clock/struct.NodeId.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/api.rs.html#72-74)

#### fn [fast_electorate](https://docs.rs#method.fast_electorate)(&self, key: &[Key](https://docs.rs/message/struct.Key.html)) -> [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[NodeId](https://docs.rs/clock/struct.NodeId.html)>

The **fast-path electorate** for `key`’s shard — the subset of
[ replicas](https://docs.rs/trait.Topology.html#tymethod.replicas) whose

`PreAccept` votes decide the
one-round-trip fast path. It is a *fixed, cluster-agreed*property of the shard (every coordinator of the shard uses the same set), placed in one region so a co-located coordinator commits in a single local round-trip.

The default is the whole replica set (no region favouring — the classic
`⌈3f/2⌉ + 1` fast path). A configured electorate must be a subset of
`replicas(key)` with `f + 1 ≤ |E| ≤ N` (asserted at construction): that
bound keeps recovery sound — a recovery quorum (`f + 1`) always intersects
a fast quorum, and any two fast quorums of the shared electorate intersect.

The shard that owns `key`. Single-shard topologies return `0`.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/api.rs.html#92-94)#### fn [node_shard](https://docs.rs#method.node_shard)(&self, _node: [NodeId](https://docs.rs/clock/struct.NodeId.html)) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[ShardId](https://docs.rs/type.ShardId.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/api.rs.html#92-94)

#### fn [node_shard](https://docs.rs#method.node_shard)(&self, _node: [NodeId](https://docs.rs/clock/struct.NodeId.html)) -> [Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[ShardId](https://docs.rs/type.ShardId.html)>

The shard `node` replicates, if any. Shards are disjoint, so a node
belongs to at most one. Single-shard topologies return `Some(0)`.

Whether `node` replicates `key` (i.e. owns its shard). Determines which
events of a multi-shard transaction a replica reads and applies.

The region / datacenter `node` lives in, if regions are configured. Used to
prefer a same-region peer (e.g. for read routing). The default is `None`
(no region awareness — all nodes treated as one locality).

Whether this topology can change epoch (reconfigure). The default is
`false` (fixed topologies); [ DynamicTopology](https://docs.rs/struct.DynamicTopology.html) overrides it to

`true`. The
node’s metadata-log catch-up sweep only runs for dynamic topologies, so a
fixed-membership cluster issues no control-plane traffic.## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait **is** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# Clock in evento_accord::clock - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/evento-accord/2.0.0-alpha.24/evento_accord/clock/trait.Clock.html

Two operations: now issues a fresh, strictly-increasing
timestamp, and witness advances this node’s clock past a
timestamp observed from a peer so that any timestamp we subsequently issue is
causally after it.

Sets the clock-skew bound — how far a witnessed peer timestamp may push this
clock beyond its own wall clock. Tune for the deployment’s expected drift
(geo links need more headroom); recovery/compaction margins should stay
above it. Defaults to [ MAX_SKEW_MICROS](https://docs.rs/constant.MAX_SKEW_MICROS.html).

# Struct Timestamp

[Source](../../src/evento_accord/clock.rs.html#27-34) ```
pub struct Timestamp {
    pub micros:
```
[u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html),
    pub logical: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html),
    pub node: [NodeId](struct.NodeId.html),
}

## Expand description

A Hybrid Logical Clock timestamp.

The field order is significant: deriving `Ord``micros` first,
then `logical`, then `node`, which is exactly the ordering Accord requires.

Wall-clock microseconds since the Unix epoch (the physical component).

Logical counter, incremented when multiple stamps share `micros`.

Issuing node — the final tie-breaker, guaranteeing global uniqueness.

The smallest possible timestamp — the initial redundancy floor (nothing is
redundant yet) and a natural lower bound.

Performs copy-assignment from

`source`.

[Read more](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/clone/trait.Clone.html#method.clone_from)

Formats the value using the given formatter.

[Read more](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Debug.html#tymethod.fmt)

Deserialize this value from the given Serde deserializer.

[Read more](https://docs.rs/serde_core/1.0.228/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/serde_core/de/trait.Deserialize.html#tymethod.deserialize)

Compares and returns the maximum of two values.

[Read more](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.Ord.html#method.max)

Compares and returns the minimum of two values.

[Read more](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.Ord.html#method.min)

Restrict a value to a certain interval.

[Read more](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.Ord.html#method.clamp)

Tests for `self` and `other` values to be equal, and is used by `==`.

Tests for `!=`. The default implementation is almost always sufficient,
and should not be overridden without very good reason.

This method returns an ordering between

`self` and

`other` values if one exists.

[Read more](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.PartialOrd.html#tymethod.partial_cmp)

Tests less than (for

`self` and

`other`) and is used by the

`<` operator.

pub struct CommandState {
    pub txn:

    pub status: [Status](https://docs.rs/enum.Status.html),
    pub promised: [Ballot](https://docs.rs/clock/struct.Ballot.html),
    pub accepted: [Ballot](https://docs.rs/clock/struct.Ballot.html),
    pub execute_at: [Timestamp](https://docs.rs/clock/struct.Timestamp.html),

## Fields[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.txn)

`txn: `[TxnId](https://docs.rs/clock/struct.TxnId.html)Transaction identity (`t0`); its node component is the coordinator.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.status)

`status: `[Status](https://docs.rs/enum.Status.html)Phase reached on this replica.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.promised)

`promised: `[Ballot](https://docs.rs/clock/struct.Ballot.html)Highest ballot promised (advanced by Accept and Recover); rejects any message carrying a lower ballot.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.accepted)

`accepted: `[Ballot](https://docs.rs/clock/struct.Ballot.html)Ballot at which `execute_at`/`deps` were last Accepted. Recovery keeps the
values from the highest accepted ballot.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.execute_at)

`execute_at: `[Timestamp](https://docs.rs/clock/struct.Timestamp.html)Agreed execution timestamp `t` (`== t0` on the fast path, `> t0` when a
conflict raised it on the slow path).

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.deps)

`deps: `[Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[TxnId](https://docs.rs/clock/struct.TxnId.html)>Transactions this one must execute after (conflicts with smaller `t0`).

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.keys)

`keys: `[Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[Key](https://docs.rs/struct.Key.html)>Keys this transaction touches (for conflict detection).

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.events)

`events: `[Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[Event](https://docs.rs/evento-core/2.0.0-alpha.24/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/evento_core/struct.Event.html)>The events this transaction conditionally appends on apply.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.reply_to)

`reply_to: `[NodeId](https://docs.rs/clock/struct.NodeId.html)Node to report the execution result to — the original coordinator, or a recovery coordinator that took over.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.decision)

`decision: `[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)>The coordinator’s commit/abort decision once known (from Apply). Recorded even if this replica is not yet ready to apply, so a lagging replica applies it as soon as its dependencies clear.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.applied_conflict)

`applied_conflict: `[Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)<[bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)>The apply outcome once executed (`Some(conflict)`), so a recoverer that
commits an already-applied transaction still learns the result.

        deps: [Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[TxnId](https://docs.rs/clock/struct.TxnId.html)>,
    },
}## Expand description

A protocol message between nodes. Every message names its transaction by
[ TxnId](https://docs.rs/clock/struct.TxnId.html); the id’s node component identifies the

*original*coordinator, so replicas route execution results back without any separate addressing.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.PreAccept)

### PreAccept

Coordinator → replicas: propose `txn` (= `t0`) for the given keys/events.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.PreAcceptOk)

### PreAcceptOk

Replica → coordinator: the timestamp this replica would execute at and
the dependencies it witnessed. The fast path succeeds when a fast quorum
all report `execute_at == t0`.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Accept)

### Accept

Coordinator → replicas (slow path / recovery): adopt the execution
timestamp and dependency set under `ballot`.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.AcceptOk)

### AcceptOk

Replica → coordinator: accepted, echoing any additional dependencies.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Commit)

### Commit

Coordinator → replicas: the execution timestamp and dependencies are
final; execute when dependencies allow. Carries events for replicas that
missed PreAccept, and `reply_to` so the execution result reaches whoever
is driving the commit (original coordinator or recoverer).

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.ReadOk)

### ReadOk

Replica → coordinator: this replica read its owned keys at the execution
timestamp; `ok` is whether their version condition holds. The coordinator
commits only if every touched shard reports `ok`.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Apply)

### Apply

Coordinator → replicas: the atomic decision. `commit` true appends the
events; false aborts the conditional write as a no-op.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Applied)

### Applied

Replica → coordinator: the decision has been durably enacted here.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Recover)

### Recover

Recovery coordinator → replicas: take over `txn` under a higher `ballot`.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.RecoverOk)

### RecoverOk

Replica → recovery coordinator: everything known about `txn`, including
the recovery-specific `superseding_rejects` signal (a later conflicting
transaction did not witness `txn`, so it cannot have taken the fast path).

#### Fields

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Nack)

### Nack

Replica → coordinator: a ballot was too low; `promised` is the ballot the
replica has already promised, so the sender can retry above it.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.SyncRequest)

### SyncRequest

Joining node → an existing replica: send me your committed state so I can
bootstrap. `snapshot` requests the materialized data-store snapshot too
(set by a bootstrapping join, whose state may be below the contact’s
truncation watermark); anti-entropy clears it (it only needs recent
commands).

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Watermark)

### Watermark

Periodic gossip between shard replicas: the sender has applied every
transaction below `applied_through`. The cluster compacts (drops redundant
consensus state and truncates the log) below the per-shard minimum of these.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.SyncData)

### SyncData

Existing replica → joining node: the committed state to import.

#### Fields

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.SyncData.field.watermark)

`watermark: `[Timestamp](https://docs.rs/clock/struct.Timestamp.html)The contact’s redundancy watermark; the joiner adopts it as its floor, so a dependency on a compacted-away transaction counts as satisfied.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.ConfigPrepare)

### ConfigPrepare

Config coordinator → acceptors: Paxos phase 1 for `epoch`’s layout.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.ConfigPromise)

### ConfigPromise

Acceptor → coordinator: promised `ballot`, reporting any value it has
already accepted (which the coordinator must adopt).

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.ConfigAccept)

### ConfigAccept

Config coordinator → acceptors: Paxos phase 2 — accept this layout.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.ConfigAccepted)

### ConfigAccepted

Acceptor → coordinator: accepted under the proposing ballot.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.ConfigCommit)

### ConfigCommit

Config coordinator → all nodes: the layout is decided; install it.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.ConfigNack)

### ConfigNack

Acceptor → coordinator: a config ballot was too low for `epoch`.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.MetadataFetch)

### MetadataFetch

A behind node → any peer: send every decided metadata-log entry strictly
after `after_epoch`, so this node can fill a gap in its topology history.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.MetadataEntries)

### MetadataEntries

A peer → the requester: contiguous decided `(epoch, layout)` entries in
ascending order (all `> after_epoch`). Fire-and-forget; the requester ingests
them, installing each now-contiguous epoch. May be empty.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.ReadForward)

### ReadForward

A node → an owner of the queried key range: serve this read locally.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.ReadReply)

### ReadReply

Owner → requester: the read result (events paired with their cursors).

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.ReadProbe)

### ReadProbe

Linearizable-read coordinator → a quorum of a key’s replicas: report the
execution timestamp and dependencies a read at `txn`’s timestamp would
witness over `key`. Unlike `PreAccept`, the replica stores **nothing** —
it is a pure query of the conflict graph (a read-index probe).

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.ReadProbeOk)

### ReadProbeOk

Replica → read coordinator: the probe’s witnessed `(execute_at, deps)`.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)
