# Status in evento_accord::message - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/evento-accord/2.0.0-alpha.24/evento_accord/message/enum.Status.html

```
pub enum Status {
    PreAccepted,
    Accepted,
    Committed,
    Reading,
    Applied,
}
```
## Expand description

How far a transaction has progressed on a given replica. Ordered so that
`>= Committed` means the execution timestamp and dependencies are final.

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.PreAccepted)

### PreAccepted

PreAccepted: replica has witnessed `t0` and reported its dependencies.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Accepted)

### Accepted

Accepted: a final execution timestamp and dependency set were agreed on the slow path (or by recovery), under some ballot.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Committed)

### Committed

Committed: execution timestamp and dependencies are final; the replica may not yet have executed.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Reading)

### Reading

Reading: dependencies are satisfied and this replica has read its owned keys and reported the version condition, but is still holding the slot awaiting the coordinator’s atomic commit/abort decision.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Applied)

### Applied

Applied: the commit/abort decision has been durably enacted.

## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/message.rs.html#37)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Copy-for-Status)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/message.rs.html#37)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Eq-for-Status)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/message.rs.html#37)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-PartialOrd-for-Status)### impl [PartialOrd](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.PartialOrd.html) for [Status](https://docs.rs/enum.Status.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/message.rs.html#37)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-PartialOrd-for-Status)

### impl [PartialOrd](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.PartialOrd.html) for [Status](https://docs.rs/enum.Status.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/message.rs.html#37)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-StructuralPartialEq-for-Status)

### impl [StructuralPartialEq](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.StructuralPartialEq.html) for [Status](https://docs.rs/enum.Status.html)

## Auto Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#synthetic-implementations)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Freeze-for-Status)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-RefUnwindSafe-for-Status)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/node.rs.html#355-367)#### pub fn [stable_micros](https://docs.rs#method.stable_micros)(&self) -> [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/node.rs.html#355-367)

#### pub fn [stable_micros](https://docs.rs#method.stable_micros)(&self) -> [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html)

Locally-safe subscription watermark, in microseconds since the Unix epoch:
every committed transaction with a `t0` below this is already applied to
the local data store, and no future transaction can be assigned a `t0`
below it (future timestamps are `>= now - max_skew`, and this trails `now`
by [ compaction_margin](https://docs.rs/struct.NodeConfig.html#structfield.compaction_margin)).

It is the same `applied_through` point the compaction sweep trusts, so a
subscription that only processes events below it cannot skip a late,
lower-cursor event applied out of order from another node — provided
propagation + clock skew stays within `compaction_margin` (the bound the
node already assumes). Exposed to [`Executor::stable_timestamp`].

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/node.rs.html#370-372)#### pub fn [metrics](https://docs.rs#method.metrics)(&self) -> [MetricsSnapshot](https://docs.rs/metrics/struct.MetricsSnapshot.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/node.rs.html#370-372)

#### pub fn [metrics](https://docs.rs#method.metrics)(&self) -> [MetricsSnapshot](https://docs.rs/metrics/struct.MetricsSnapshot.html)

A point-in-time snapshot of this node’s observability counters.

Spawns the inbox loop that drives this node until the network closes.

**Group commit:** each iteration drains up to
[ max_journal_batch](https://docs.rs/struct.NodeConfig.html#structfield.max_journal_batch) already-
queued messages, stages each one’s durable writes, flushes the journal

**once**for the whole batch, then performs the deferred (durability-gated) sends. Under load a burst of consensus messages costs a single fsync; with one message in flight it behaves exactly as a per-message sync.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/node.rs.html#426-434)#### pub fn [start_recovery](https://docs.rs#method.start_recovery)(&self) -> [JoinHandle](https://docs.rs/tokio/1.52.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/tokio/runtime/task/join/struct.JoinHandle.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/node.rs.html#426-434)

#### pub fn [start_recovery](https://docs.rs#method.start_recovery)(&self) -> [JoinHandle](https://docs.rs/tokio/1.52.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/tokio/runtime/task/join/struct.JoinHandle.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html)>

Spawns the automatic-recovery sweep: periodically takes over any
transaction that has stalled (its coordinator presumed dead) and drives it
to completion, so a crashed coordinator can never block progress forever.
Opt-in — call alongside [ start](https://docs.rs/struct.Node.html#method.start) on a real deployment.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/node.rs.html#441-489)#### pub async fn [recover_state](https://docs.rs#method.recover_state)(&self) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/anyhow/1.0.103/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/anyhow/type.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/node.rs.html#441-489)

#### pub async fn [recover_state](https://docs.rs#method.recover_state)(&self) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/anyhow/1.0.103/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/anyhow/type.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html)>

Rebuilds this node’s state from the journal after a process restart:
restores every command’s consensus state (status, ballots, decision) and
replays committed, applied transactions into the data store. Call once on
startup before [ start](https://docs.rs/struct.Node.html#method.start). In-flight (unapplied) transactions
resume via the recovery sweep.

Compacts consensus state below `before`: drops redundant commands from the
in-memory replica and truncates the journal, bounding both to in-flight
work. `before` must be a **cluster-safe** watermark — every replica has
applied everything below it (the recovery sweep computes this as the
per-shard minimum; supplied directly here and in tests). The journal is
truncated to the replica’s *actual* resulting watermark, which `compact`
may clamp below `before` if a local transaction is not yet applied.

Coordinates appending `events` as one strictly-serializable, atomic
transaction across every shard it touches.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/node.rs.html#1231-1286)#### pub async fn [read_barrier](https://docs.rs#method.read_barrier)(&self, key: [Key](https://docs.rs/message/struct.Key.html)) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/anyhow/1.0.103/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/anyhow/type.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/node.rs.html#1231-1286)

#### pub async fn [read_barrier](https://docs.rs#method.read_barrier)(&self, key: [Key](https://docs.rs/message/struct.Key.html)) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/anyhow/1.0.103/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/anyhow/type.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html)>

A **linearizable read barrier** for one owned `key`, as a lightweight
**read-index** (it stores nothing and is never journaled — a read never
enters the conflict graph):

- Probe a slow quorum (`f + 1`) of the key’s replicas for the dependencies a read at a fresh timestamp would witness (`ReadProbe`
- Wait until every witnessed dependency is **applied locally**(`Replica::deps_applied`

A subsequent local read of `key` then reflects every write that committed
before the barrier began — i.e. it is linearizable. The caller must own
`key` (be a replica) so the local wait actually fences its reads. Errors
(quorum unreachable, or a dependency that never applies in time) surface
as an unavailable read rather than a stale one.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/node.rs.html#1525-1730)#### pub async fn [recover](https://docs.rs#method.recover)(&self, txn: [TxnId](https://docs.rs/clock/struct.TxnId.html)) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/anyhow/1.0.103/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/anyhow/type.Result.html)<[CommitOutcome](https://docs.rs/struct.CommitOutcome.html)>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/node.rs.html#1525-1730)

#### pub async fn [recover](https://docs.rs#method.recover)(&self, txn: [TxnId](https://docs.rs/clock/struct.TxnId.html)) -> [Result](https://docs.rs/anyhow/1.0.103/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/anyhow/type.Result.html)<[CommitOutcome](https://docs.rs/struct.CommitOutcome.html)>

Recovers `txn`: takes it over under a fresh ballot and drives it to an
applied outcome consistent with whatever its failed coordinator decided.

Runs only PreAccept and returns the transaction id, modelling a
coordinator that crashed before committing. For tests of [`recover`].

Bootstraps this (joining) node from `contact`: fetches its committed state,
imports every command for a key this node now owns (recording it in the
conflict graph and applying its events), then replays any consensus
messages buffered since [ begin_join](https://docs.rs/struct.Node.html#method.begin_join) — so a transaction
committed during the join still lands. Returns how many were imported.

Coordinating the epoch change across the cluster (rather than each node installing an agreed layout) remains future work.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/node.rs.html#1888-1897)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/node.rs.html#1888-1897)

Coordinates installing `shards` as the new `epoch`’s layout, fault
tolerantly: runs single-decree Paxos over the **current members** so the
decision survives this coordinator failing, then commits it cluster-wide.
Returns the decided layout (which differs from `shards` only if a prior,
interrupted change for this epoch had already been accepted).

The acceptor set is the members of the current epoch (a node proposing the next epoch is still on this one), so it tracks membership: changes keep working after the original founders have left.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/node.rs.html#1902-1909)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/node.rs.html#1902-1909)

Drives Paxos phases 1–2 for `epoch` (no commit), returning the decided
layout. Exposed so tests can simulate a coordinator that fails after the
decision is durable but before committing.

Recovers a possibly-interrupted change for `epoch`: completes whatever
layout was already accepted (or, if none was, keeps the current layout),
then commits it. Any node can call this after the original coordinator
fails.

Whether this node replicates `key` (and so can serve reads for it locally).

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/node.rs.html#2180-2191)

# NodeConfig in evento_accord::node - Rust

```
pub struct NodeConfig {
    pub fast_timeout:
```
[Duration](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/time/struct.Duration.html),
    pub collect_timeout: [Duration](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/time/struct.Duration.html),
    pub recovery_interval: [Duration](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/time/struct.Duration.html),
    pub recovery_timeout: [Duration](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/time/struct.Duration.html),
    pub compaction_margin: [Duration](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/time/struct.Duration.html),
    pub max_journal_batch: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html),
    pub phi_threshold: [f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f64.html),
    pub linearizable_reads: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html),
    pub max_commands: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html),
    pub config_defer_step: [Duration](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/time/struct.Duration.html),
}## Expand description

Tunable timing/sizing parameters for a [ Node](https://docs.rs/struct.Node.html).

[reproduces the values the cluster shipped with; geo deployments raise the timeouts to match cross-region round-trips. (The clock-skew bound lives on the injected](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/default/trait.Default.html)

`Default`[— see](https://docs.rs/clock/struct.HybridLogicalClock.html)

`HybridLogicalClock``with_max_skew` — since only the clock reads it.)## Fields[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.fast_timeout)

`fast_timeout: `[Duration](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/time/struct.Duration.html)Wait for the fast quorum before falling back to the slow path. Short so a down node barely delays a write.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.collect_timeout)

`collect_timeout: `[Duration](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/time/struct.Duration.html)Cap on waiting for a slow quorum at later phases (returns as soon as the quorum is reached; the cap only bounds a genuinely stuck phase).

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.recovery_interval)

`recovery_interval: `[Duration](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/time/struct.Duration.html)How often the automatic-recovery sweep runs.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.recovery_timeout)

`recovery_timeout: `[Duration](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/time/struct.Duration.html)A transaction unapplied this long is presumed stalled and recovered. Well above normal write latency so healthy in-flight writes are never disturbed.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.compaction_margin)

`compaction_margin: `[Duration](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/time/struct.Duration.html)How far behind the present a node’s reported redundancy point lags, so a not-yet-propagated commit is never skipped when state below the watermark is compacted away. Keep it above the clock-skew bound and propagation latency.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.max_journal_batch)

`max_journal_batch: `[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)Most messages the inbox loop stages before forcing a group-commit flush. Caps the latency a deferred reply waits for its batch’s fsync and the memory held for the batch’s pending sends.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.phi_threshold)

`phi_threshold: `[f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f64.html)Suspicion threshold for the phi-accrual failure detector: a coordinator
whose φ exceeds this is presumed dead and its stalled transactions are
recovered (adaptively, ahead of `recovery_timeout`). Higher tolerates more
latency variance before suspecting.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.linearizable_reads)

`linearizable_reads: `[bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)Serve **linearizable** reads of a single owned key by coordinating a
read-only barrier transaction (`Node::read_barrier`) before reading the
local backend, instead of reading possibly-stale local state directly.
Costs one consensus round per read; off by default (reads stay local and
fast, but are only serializable — a read off a lagging replica can break
real-time order).

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.max_commands)

`max_commands: `[usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)Backpressure on the consensus backlog: if this node already holds at least
this many un-compacted commands, it **refuses to coordinate a new write**
(returning an error) rather than letting `Replica.commands` grow without bound
— e.g. under a sustained partition where compaction stalls. Only the local
coordinator’s new-write entry point is gated; replica-side handling of peer
consensus messages is never refused (that would break safety/liveness). Set
high enough to never trip in a healthy cluster.

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.config_defer_step)

`config_defer_step: `[Duration](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/time/struct.Duration.html)Control-plane anti-dueling delay. An automatic config-change recovery defers
by `rank * config_defer_step` (the **distinguished proposer** for an epoch has
rank 0 and proposes first; others wait, then skip if it already committed), and
a ballot duel backs off by a rank/attempt-derived multiple of this — so
concurrent reconfigurations converge instead of livelocking. Deterministic
(no RNG), so the simulation stays bit-reproducible.

# InMemoryDataStore in evento_accord::store - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/evento-accord/2.0.0-alpha.24/evento_accord/store/struct.InMemoryDataStore.html

`pub struct InMemoryDataStore { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

In-memory applied event store for one replica.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

### impl [DataStore](https://docs.rs/api/trait.DataStore.html) for [InMemoryDataStore](https://docs.rs/struct.InMemoryDataStore.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/store.rs.html#76-83)[§](https://docs.rs#method.version)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/store.rs.html#76-83)

[§](https://docs.rs#method.version)

Current version of an aggregate. Returns 0 for an aggregate with no
events. Used during the Read phase to evaluate the optimistic-version
condition before any shard appends.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/store.rs.html#85-115)[§](https://docs.rs#method.apply)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/store.rs.html#85-115)

[§](https://docs.rs#method.apply)

Records a decided transaction at its execution timestamp. When

`commit` is true the `events` are appended (advancing versions);
otherwise the transaction is a no-op (an aborted conditional write).
Implementations must apply in `execute_at` order to preserve the global
serial order. `events` is only this replica’s owned subset.[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/store.rs.html#117-130)[§](https://docs.rs#method.snapshot)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/store.rs.html#117-130)

[§](https://docs.rs#method.snapshot)

All applied events materialised in this store — the bootstrap snapshot a
joining node installs to reconstruct the state that log truncation has
removed from the command journal. The default is empty (a store whose
journal never truncates needs no snapshot).

    'life0: 'async_trait,

Serves a read query from the local backend, so a node can answer reads
forwarded to it for a key range it owns. The default returns nothing (a
store that holds no queryable events, e.g. the in-memory test store).

# InMemoryJournal in evento_accord::store - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/evento-accord/2.0.0-alpha.24/evento_accord/store/struct.InMemoryJournal.html

`pub struct InMemoryJournal { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

In-memory [ Journal](https://docs.rs/api/trait.Journal.html). Records each command’s durable state as it advances;
process-restart replay from the journal is future work, so for now it is
exercised but not yet relied upon for recovery (which uses live replica state).

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/store.rs.html#156-235)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-Journal-for-InMemoryJournal)

### impl [Journal](https://docs.rs/api/trait.Journal.html) for [InMemoryJournal](https://docs.rs/struct.InMemoryJournal.html)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/store.rs.html#165-172)[§](https://docs.rs#method.load)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/store.rs.html#165-172)

[§](https://docs.rs#method.load)

Loads the persisted state for

`txn`, if any.[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/store.rs.html#174-182)[§](https://docs.rs#method.load_all)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/store.rs.html#174-182)

[§](https://docs.rs#method.load_all)

All persisted command states, for rebuilding replica state after a
process restart. The default returns nothing (a non-durable journal).

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/store.rs.html#184-191)[§](https://docs.rs#method.truncate)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/store.rs.html#184-191)

[§](https://docs.rs#method.truncate)

Discards every record whose transaction is below

`before` (its
transactions are redundant — applied on every replica) and persists
`before` as the truncation watermark, so a restart sets its redundancy
floor and trusts the data store for everything below it. Bounds the log to
in-flight work. The default is a no-op (a non-truncating journal).[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/store.rs.html#193-195)[§](https://docs.rs#method.load_watermark)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/store.rs.html#193-195)

[§](https://docs.rs#method.load_watermark)

The persisted truncation watermark, if any — the redundancy floor a restart
restores. The default returns nothing.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/store.rs.html#197-206)[§](https://docs.rs#method.append_metadata)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/store.rs.html#197-206)

[§](https://docs.rs#method.append_metadata)

Durably appends a decided metadata-log entry — one

`epoch`’s committed
topology `layout`. Durable by the time it returns. Idempotent: re-appending
an epoch already present with the same layout is a no-op. The default is a
no-op (a journal that does not back dynamic membership).[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/store.rs.html#208-216)[§](https://docs.rs#method.load_metadata)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/evento_accord/store.rs.html#208-216)

[§](https://docs.rs#method.load_metadata)

All persisted metadata-log entries, ascending by epoch, for replaying the
committed topology sequence after a restart. The default returns nothing.

Durably persists this node’s config-Paxos acceptor state for one

`epoch`.
Durable by the time it returns — this is the crash-safety gate (a restarted
acceptor must not promise/accept a ballot lower than one already promised).

# serve in evento_accord::tcp - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/evento-accord/2.0.0-alpha.24/evento_accord/tcp/fn.serve.html

# Function serve

[Source](../../src/evento_accord/tcp.rs.html#277-284) `pub fn serve(listener: `[TcpListener](https://docs.rs/tokio/1.52.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/tokio/net/tcp/listener/struct.TcpListener.html), inbox: [Sender](https://docs.rs/tokio/1.52.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/tokio/sync/mpsc/bounded/struct.Sender.html)<[Envelope](../transport/struct.Envelope.html)>) -> [JoinHandle](https://docs.rs/tokio/1.52.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/tokio/runtime/task/join/struct.JoinHandle.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html)>

## Expand description

Accepts inbound connections on `listener`, decoding frames and forwarding
each as an `Envelope``inbox`. Returns the accept-loop task handle.

# serve_tls in evento_accord::tcp - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/evento-accord/2.0.0-alpha.24/evento_accord/tcp/fn.serve_tls.html

```
pub fn serve_tls(
    listener:
```
[TcpListener](https://docs.rs/tokio/1.52.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/tokio/net/tcp/listener/struct.TcpListener.html),
    inbox: [Sender](https://docs.rs/tokio/1.52.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/tokio/sync/mpsc/bounded/struct.Sender.html)<[Envelope](https://docs.rs/transport/struct.Envelope.html)>,
    acceptor: [TlsAcceptor](https://docs.rs/tokio-rustls/0.26.4/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/tokio_rustls/server/struct.TlsAcceptor.html),
) -> [JoinHandle](https://docs.rs/tokio/1.52.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/tokio/runtime/task/join/struct.JoinHandle.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html)>## Expand description

Like [ serve](https://docs.rs/fn.serve.html) but completes a TLS handshake (

`acceptor`, with client-cert
verification for mutual TLS) on each inbound connection before reading frames.
The wire `from` is **trusted**— for a trusted network, or where every node shares one certificate. Use

[to authenticate per-node identity instead.](https://docs.rs/fn.serve_tls_verified.html)

`serve_tls_verified`

---

    acceptor: [TlsAcceptor](https://docs.rs/tokio-rustls/0.26.4/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/tokio_rustls/server/struct.TlsAcceptor.html),
    peers: [PeerCerts](https://docs.rs/type.PeerCerts.html),
) -> [JoinHandle](https://docs.rs/tokio/1.52.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/tokio/runtime/task/join/struct.JoinHandle.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html)>## Expand description

Like [ serve_tls](https://docs.rs/fn.serve_tls.html) but

**authenticates each peer’s identity**by pinning: after the handshake the client’s presented leaf certificate must equal one of

`peers`,
and the matched [—](https://docs.rs/clock/struct.NodeId.html)

`NodeId`*not*the self-declared wire

`from` — is stamped on
every [. A connection whose certificate matches no pin is dropped, so a CA-valid outsider cannot join, and no node can frame messages as another.](https://docs.rs/transport/struct.Envelope.html)

`Envelope`

# TlsClient in evento_accord::tcp - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/evento-accord/2.0.0-alpha.24/evento_accord/tcp/struct.TlsClient.html

`pub struct TlsClient { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Client-side TLS settings: the rustls connector and the server name presented
for certificate verification. Optionally **pins** each peer’s leaf certificate
(`with_peer_certs`), so the client only trusts a dialed peer if it presents
exactly that node’s certificate — defeating a CA-valid impostor at the address.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Registers `node` and returns its (bounded) inbox receiver. Call once per
node before sending; re-registering replaces the previous inbox.

Severs the link between `a` and `b` in both directions (a partition).

Sets the one-way delivery latency on the directed link `from → to`. Zero

# evento_accord::clock - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/evento-accord/2.0.0-alpha.24/evento_accord/clock/index.html

## Expand description

Cluster node identity and the Hybrid Logical Clock.

Accord names and orders every transaction by a globally unique,
monotonically increasing [ Timestamp](https://docs.rs/struct.Timestamp.html). Uniqueness comes from the triple

`(micros, logical, node)`: `node` breaks ties between stamps issued in the
same microsecond on different nodes, and `logical` breaks ties on the same
node. The [trait abstracts time so the simulation harness can drive it deterministically;](https://docs.rs/trait.Clock.html)

`Clock`[is the production implementation.](https://docs.rs/struct.HybridLogicalClock.html)

`HybridLogicalClock`## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Ballot](https://docs.rs/struct.Ballot.html)
- A recovery ballot, used to fence stale coordinators during the recovery
protocol (M2). Higher ballots win; a fresh transaction starts at ballot
equal to its `t0`.
- [Hybrid](https://docs.rs/struct.HybridLogicalClock.html)- Logical - Clock
- Production `Clock``NodeId`
- [NodeId](https://docs.rs/struct.NodeId.html)
- Identifier for a node in the cluster.
- [Timestamp](https://docs.rs/struct.Timestamp.html)
- A Hybrid Logical Clock timestamp.
- [TxnId](https://docs.rs/struct.TxnId.html)
- The identity of a transaction.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [MAX_](https://docs.rs/constant.MAX_SKEW_MICROS.html)- SKEW_ - MICROS
- Maximum clock skew the Hybrid Logical Clock will adopt from a peer. A
witnessed timestamp more than this far beyond the local wall clock is capped,
so a faulty/far-future timestamp cannot run the clock away. Recovery and
compaction margins (`RECOVERY_TIMEOUT`,`COMPACTION_MARGIN`in`node.rs`) are kept comfortably above this so the bounded residual skew is absorbed.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Clock](https://docs.rs/trait.Clock.html)
- Abstract monotonic clock.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [system_](https://docs.rs/fn.system_micros.html)- micros
- Wall-clock microseconds since the Unix epoch (0 if the system clock is before
the epoch, which should never happen in practice). The default physical-time
source for `HybridLogicalClock`

---

# evento_accord::executor - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/evento-accord/2.0.0-alpha.24/evento_accord/executor/index.html

## Expand description

Wiring Accord into evento’s [ Executor](https://docs.rs/evento-core/2.0.0-alpha.24/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/evento_core/executor/trait.Executor.html) trait.

[ AccordExecutor](https://docs.rs/struct.AccordExecutor.html) is a drop-in

`evento_core::Executor` whose **writes**are coordinated through an Accord cluster — replicated, strictly serializable, and atomic across aggregates — while

**reads, subscriptions, and snapshots**are served from a local evento backend (

`Fjall`/`Sql`) that each replica keeps up
to date by applying committed transactions.[ ExecutorDataStore](https://docs.rs/struct.ExecutorDataStore.html) is the bridge in the other direction: the Accord

[that a replica uses to read an aggregate’s version (for the commit condition) and to append committed events — both delegated to that same local backend. Share one backend instance (it is](https://docs.rs/api/trait.DataStore.html)

`DataStore``Clone`/`Arc`-backed) between the two so a node’s writes are visible to
its reads.[§](https://docs.rs#scope)Scope

This targets a **single-shard** cluster (every node replicates everything),
so a node’s local backend holds the whole log and serves complete reads.
Routing reads to owning shards in a multi-shard cluster is a later layer.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Accord](https://docs.rs/struct.AccordExecutor.html)- Executor
- An evento `Executor`
- [Executor](https://docs.rs/struct.ExecutorDataStore.html)- Data - Store
- An Accord `DataStore``Executor`

---

# evento_accord::format - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/evento-accord/2.0.0-alpha.24/evento_accord/format/index.html

## Expand description

On-the-wire and on-disk record framing: a small, explicit version tag in front of every bitcode payload, so a format change is detectable instead of silently mis-parsed.

bitcode is **positional and not self-describing**: a field added to or reordered
in [ CommandState](https://docs.rs/message/struct.CommandState.html) or

[would deserialize old bytes into garbage rather than fail. The 4-byte header here guards that boundary — magic + format version + a record-kind discriminant — so a reader rejects anything it does not understand.](https://docs.rs/message/enum.Message.html)

`Message````
┌────────┬────────┬──────────────┬──────────────────────────┐
│ MAGIC  │ format │  RecordKind  │   bitcode payload …       │
│ 2 byte │ 1 byte │   1 byte     │                           │
└────────┴────────┴──────────────┴──────────────────────────┘
```
[§](https://docs.rs#scope)Scope

Only the **bitcode boundary** is tagged: the framed-TCP wire ([ crate::tcp](https://docs.rs/tcp/index.html)) and
the disk journal

*values*([

`crate::fjall_journal`]). The in-memory transport and
journal pass typed structs by value and never serialize, so they are untouched.
Journal **keys**are likewise left bare (a

`TxnId` whose ordering the journal’s
truncation scan relies on); the value carries the schema that evolves.[§](https://docs.rs#rolling-upgrade-path)Rolling-upgrade path

The tag is what makes a future format change *safe*, not a compatibility layer for
the past — this is a pre-1.0 alpha, so today’s tag is mandatory and there is no
reader for untagged records (an operator upgrading from an untagged build wipes the
journal and re-bootstraps via `join`, which transfers a fresh snapshot).

- **Wire:**a node on a newer- `FORMAT_VERSION`- *shed*each other’s frames (decode returns- `Err`, and the inbound loop already drops un-decodable frames — loss the consensus layer tolerates). So a cluster rolls- **drain-and-replace**: keep a quorum on one version at a time; never restart every node onto a breaking format at once.
- **Journal:**to add a field, bump- `FORMAT_VERSION`- `decode_tagged`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Record](https://docs.rs/enum.RecordKind.html)- Kind
- Which payload schema a tagged record carries. Lets the wire frame and the two journal value-types share one codec while staying independently identifiable, so a journal value can never be mistaken for a wire frame or vice versa.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [FORMAT_](https://docs.rs/constant.FORMAT_VERSION.html)- VERSION
- Current record format version. Bump on any breaking change to a tagged payload’s
layout (a new/reordered `CommandState``Message`
- [MAGIC](https://docs.rs/constant.MAGIC.html)
- Identifies an evento-accord record. Guards against decoding an unrelated byte stream (a misconfigured port, a different protocol) as a valid frame.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_tagged.html)- tagged
- Deserializes a tagged record, validating the header first. Fails loudly — bad magic, an unknown format version, or a mismatched kind all error rather than risk decoding the payload under the wrong schema.
- [encode_](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_tagged.html)- tagged
- Serializes `value`as a tagged record: the 4-byte header followed by its bitcode encoding.

# evento_accord::message - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/evento-accord/2.0.0-alpha.24/evento_accord/message/index.html

## Expand description

Wire messages and per-transaction command state.

The protocol vocabulary: the PreAccept → Accept → Commit → Read → Apply
phases (ballot-fenced), plus the recovery exchange (`Recover` / `RecoverOk` /
`Nack`) a live node uses to take over a transaction whose coordinator is
presumed dead. `Commit` carries the events so a replica that missed PreAccept
(it was slow or down) can still apply, and the per-shard dependency set for
that shard’s execution barrier.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Command](https://docs.rs/struct.CommandState.html)- State
- A replica’s knowledge of one transaction — the unit the
`Journal`
- [Key](https://docs.rs/struct.Key.html)
- Sharding / ownership unit. Derived from an event’s routing key (falling back
to its aggregate id), this is what the `Topology`*conflict*when they share a key.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Message](https://docs.rs/enum.Message.html)
- A protocol message between nodes. Every message names its transaction by
`TxnId`*original*coordinator, so replicas route execution results back without any separate addressing.
- [Status](https://docs.rs/enum.Status.html)
- How far a transaction has progressed on a given replica. Ordered so that
`>= Committed`means the execution timestamp and dependencies are final.

[(e.g. to export to a metrics backend, or to assert behaviour in tests). Paired with the](https://docs.rs/struct.Metrics.html#method.snapshot)

`Metrics::snapshot``tracing` events the node emits at the same decision points.## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

# evento_accord::replica - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/evento-accord/2.0.0-alpha.24/evento_accord/replica/index.html

## Expand description

Replica-side consensus state machine.

A [ Replica](https://docs.rs/struct.Replica.html) tracks every transaction it has witnessed and the conflict
graph between them. It is deliberately synchronous and side-effect free:

[owns it behind a lock, calls these methods to mutate consensus state, and performs the asynchronous data-store reads and applies that](https://docs.rs/node/struct.Node.html)

`Node`[and](https://docs.rs/struct.Replica.html#method.next_read)

`next_read`[schedule.](https://docs.rs/struct.Replica.html#method.next_apply)

`next_apply`[§](https://docs.rs#timestamps-and-dependencies)Timestamps and dependencies

On PreAccept a replica computes an execution timestamp for the transaction:
`t0` if no conflicting transaction has a higher one, otherwise the smallest
timestamp (carrying the transaction’s own coordinator id) that exceeds every
conflict. Its dependencies are the conflicting transactions whose `t0` is
below that execution timestamp.

[§](https://docs.rs#ballots-and-recovery)Ballots and recovery

Each command tracks a `promised` ballot (advanced by Accept and Recover) and
the `accepted` ballot of its current execute-at/deps. A message carrying a
lower ballot is rejected so a stale coordinator cannot overwrite a recovered
decision. [ recover](https://docs.rs/struct.Replica.html#method.recover) reports a replica’s knowledge plus

`superseding_rejects`: whether a later conflicting transaction failed to
witness this one, which proves it could not have committed on the fast path.## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Apply](https://docs.rs/struct.ApplyReady.html)- Ready
- A transaction with a recorded decision whose dependencies are satisfied,
ready for the node to enact (append if `commit`, else abort).
- [Ready](https://docs.rs/struct.Ready.html)
- A transaction whose dependencies are satisfied and that the node should now
read (and later apply). The `Reading`
- [Recover](https://docs.rs/struct.RecoverState.html)- State
- What a replica reports when asked to recover a transaction.
- [Replica](https://docs.rs/struct.Replica.html)
- Per-replica consensus state.

---

# evento_accord::store - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/evento-accord/2.0.0-alpha.24/evento_accord/store/index.html

## Expand description

In-memory [ DataStore](https://docs.rs/api/trait.DataStore.html) and

[for tests and the simulation harness.](https://docs.rs/api/trait.Journal.html)

`Journal`The data store mirrors evento’s optimistic-concurrency rule — a unique
constraint on `(aggregate_type, aggregate_id, version)` — by rejecting an
append whose version is already taken for that aggregate. Because the node
applies committed transactions strictly in execution-timestamp order, two
racing same-version appends deterministically resolve to one winner.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Applied](https://docs.rs/struct.AppliedEntry.html)- Entry
- One applied transaction, recorded so tests can assert that every replica produced the same global serial order and the same conflict outcomes.
- [InMemory](https://docs.rs/struct.InMemoryDataStore.html)- Data - Store
- In-memory applied event store for one replica.
- [InMemory](https://docs.rs/struct.InMemoryJournal.html)- Journal
- In-memory `Journal`

# rship-sync 4.0.0-canary.64 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rship-sync/4.0.0-canary.64

Sync Value System

High-precision synchronized value distribution using hyphae cells. Runs in-process with a 240Hz master clock for value updates.

# Usage

```
use rship_sync::{context, ValueRunnerRegistry, SyncValueConfig};
use std::sync::Arc;
// Initialize (once at startup)
let registry = Arc::new(ValueRunnerRegistry::new());
context::init(registry);
// Create and watch values
rship_sync::ensure_value("my/value", &SyncValueConfig { value: 0.0, rate: 1.0, running: true }, 30.0);
let cell = rship_sync::watch_value("my/value");
```

# hyphae - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/hyphae/^1.0.2/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#hyphae---lock-free-reactive-programming-library)hyphae - Lock-Free Reactive Programming Library

A high-performance, type-safe reactive programming library featuring true lock-free operations, heterogeneous cell combinations, and comprehensive dependency tracking.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- **Lock-Free**: Uses- `arc-swap`for atomic value updates without blocking
- **Type-Safe**: Full compile-time type checking with heterogeneous cell support
- **Automatic Propagation**: Changes flow through dependency chains automatically
- **Dependency Tracking**: Inspect and visualize cell relationships
- **Thread-Safe**: Safe concurrent access across threads

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

```
use hyphae::{Cell, MapExt, MaterializeDefinite, Mutable, Watchable, JoinExt, Pipeline, Signal, flat};
// Create reactive cells
let x = Cell::new(5).with_name("x");
let y = Cell::new(10).with_name("y");
// Pure operators (map/filter/...) return pipelines — no allocation
// until you materialize.
let doubled = x.clone().map(|val| val * 2).materialize().with_name("doubled");
// Combine multiple cells with join + flat!. join is stateful — it
// returns a Cell directly. Chaining .map fuses into the join's
// installed callback when materialized.
let sum = x.join(&y).map(flat!(|a, b| a + b)).materialize().with_name("sum");
// Subscribe on the materialized cell
let _guard = sum.subscribe(|signal| {
    if let Signal::Value(value) = signal {
        println!("Sum changed to: {}", value);
    }
});
x.set(20); // Triggers updates
```
[§](https://docs.rs#pipelines-vs-cells)Pipelines vs Cells

Pure operators (`map`, `filter`, `try_map`, `tap`, `map_ok`, `map_err`,
`catch_error`, `unwrap_or`) return a [ Pipeline](https://docs.rs/pipeline/trait.Pipeline.html) — an uncompiled chain
that has not yet been materialized into a

[. Chaining pipelines fuses closures at compile time; the fused closure runs only when a consumer calls [](https://docs.rs/cell/struct.Cell.html)

`Cell``Pipeline::materialize`].[ Cell](https://docs.rs/cell/struct.Cell.html) is the materialized, cached, multicast form. Subscribing requires
a cell — there is no

`Pipeline::subscribe` by design, forcing callers to
make the memoization decision explicit.Stateful operators (`scan`, `debounce`, `throttle`, `buffer_*`, `pairwise`,
`window`, `distinct*`, `sample`, `delay`, `take`, `first`, `last`, `merge`,
`merge_map`, `switch_map`, `with_latest_from`, `zip`, `join`) return cells
directly — they hold per-subscription state, so memoization is unavoidable.

[§](https://docs.rs#combining-cells)Combining Cells

Use `join()` to combine cells, and the `flat!` macro to avoid nested tuple destructuring.
`join` is stateful and returns a [ Cell](https://docs.rs/cell/struct.Cell.html) directly, so the chain below is a cell
once

`.map(...)` fuses onto it — no `.materialize()` needed for `.get()`:```
use hyphae::{Cell, Gettable, JoinExt, MapExt, MaterializeDefinite, flat};
let a = Cell::new(1);
let b = Cell::new(2);
let c = Cell::new(3);
let d = Cell::new(4);
// Without flat!: |(((a, b), c), d)| - deeply nested
// With flat!: |a, b, c, d| - clean and simple
let sum = a
    .join(&b)
    .join(&c)
    .join(&d)
    .map(flat!(|a, b, c, d| a + b + c + d))
    .materialize();
assert_eq!(sum.get(), 10);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#map-queries-vs-cellmaps)Map Queries vs CellMaps

Pure [ CellMap](https://docs.rs/cell_map/struct.CellMap.html) operators (

`inner_join`, `left_join`, `left_semi_join`,
`multi_left_join`, `project`, `project_many`, `project_cell`, `select`,
`select_cell`, `count_by`, `group_by`) return uncompiled [plan nodes — not](https://docs.rs/map_query/trait.MapQuery.html)

`MapQuery`[s. A plan tree composes freely: any plan or](https://docs.rs/cell_map/struct.CellMap.html)

`CellMap`[can feed any other operator’s input.](https://docs.rs/cell_map/struct.CellMap.html)

`CellMap`Calling [ MapQuery::materialize](https://docs.rs/map_query/trait.MapQuery.html#method.materialize) allocates ONE output

[with ONE subscription per root source running the fully fused diff-propagation closure. This replaces what used to be N intermediate](https://docs.rs/cell_map/struct.CellMap.html)

`CellMap`[s, N subscriber tables, and N](https://docs.rs/cell_map/struct.CellMap.html)

`CellMap``ArcSwap` chains for an N-stage query.[ MapQuery](https://docs.rs/map_query/trait.MapQuery.html) plan nodes are deliberately not

`Clone` (mirroring
[). Cloning would silently duplicate join / projection work — every clone’s](https://docs.rs/pipeline/trait.Pipeline.html)

`Pipeline``materialize()` would install independent root subscriptions
and re-run the entire op chain. To share work across consumers,
materialize once into a [(which IS](https://docs.rs/cell_map/struct.CellMap.html)

`CellMap``Clone` — the clone is an
`Arc` bump referencing the same multicast cache) and then clone the cell
map.[§](https://docs.rs#cellmap-quick-start)CellMap Quick Start

```
use hyphae::{CellMap, MapQuery, traits::{InnerJoinExt, ProjectMapExt}};
let users = CellMap::<String, &'static str>::new();
let scores = CellMap::<String, i32>::new();
users.insert("u1".into(), "alice");
scores.insert("u1".into(), 42);
// Chained operators return plan nodes — no intermediate CellMap
// until materialize().
let view = users
    .clone()
    .inner_join(scores.clone())
    .project(|user_id, (name, score)| Some((user_id.clone(), format!("{name}:{score}"))))
    .materialize();
assert!(view.contains_key(&"u1".to_string()));
```

# log - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/log/^0.4/

## Expand description

A lightweight logging facade.

The `log` crate provides a single logging API that abstracts over the
actual logging implementation. Libraries can use the logging API provided
by this crate, and the consumer of those libraries can choose the logging
implementation that is most suitable for its use case.

If no logging implementation is selected, the facade falls back to a “noop” implementation that ignores all log messages. The overhead in this case is very small - just an integer load, comparison and jump.

A log request consists of a *target*, a *level*, and a *body*. A target is a
string which defaults to the module path of the location of the log request,
though that default may be overridden. Logger implementations typically use
the target to filter requests based on some user configuration.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

The basic use of the log crate is through the five logging macros: [ error!](https://docs.rs/macro.error.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/macro.warn.html)

`warn!`[,](https://docs.rs/macro.info.html)

`info!`[and](https://docs.rs/macro.debug.html)

`debug!`[where](https://docs.rs/macro.trace.html)

`trace!``error!` represents the highest-priority log messages
and `trace!` the lowest. The log messages are filtered by configuring
the log level to exclude messages with a lower priority.
Each of these macros accept format strings similarly to [.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/macro.println.html)

`println!`Avoid writing expressions with side-effects in log statements. They may not be evaluated.

[§](https://docs.rs#in-libraries)In libraries

Libraries should link only to the `log` crate, and use the provided
macros to log whatever information will be useful to downstream consumers.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use log::{info, warn};
pub fn shave_the_yak(yak: &mut Yak) {
    info!(target: "yak_events", "Commencing yak shaving for {yak:?}");
    loop {
        match find_a_razor() {
            Ok(razor) => {
                info!("Razor located: {razor}");
                yak.shave(razor);
                break;
            }
            Err(err) => {
                warn!("Unable to locate a razor: {err}, retrying");
            }
        }
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#in-executables)In executables

Executables should choose a logging implementation and initialize it early in the runtime of the program. Logging implementations will typically include a function to do this. Any log messages generated before the implementation is initialized will be ignored.

The executable itself may use the `log` crate to log as well.

[§](https://docs.rs#warning)Warning

The logging system may only be initialized once.

[§](https://docs.rs#structured-logging)Structured logging

If you enable the `kv` feature you can associate structured values
with your log records. If we take the example from before, we can include
some additional context besides what’s in the formatted message:

```
use log::{info, warn};
pub fn shave_the_yak(yak: &mut Yak) {
    info!(target: "yak_events", yak:serde; "Commencing yak shaving");
    loop {
        match find_a_razor() {
            Ok(razor) => {
                info!(razor; "Razor located");
                yak.shave(razor);
                break;
            }
            Err(e) => {
                warn!(e:err; "Unable to locate a razor, retrying");
            }
        }
    }
}
```
See the [ kv](https://docs.rs/kv/index.html) module documentation for more details.

[§](https://docs.rs#available-logging-implementations)Available logging implementations

In order to produce log output executables have to use a logger implementation compatible with the facade. There are many available implementations to choose from, here are some of the most popular ones:

- Simple minimal loggers:
- Complex configurable frameworks:
- Adaptors for other facilities:
- For WebAssembly binaries:
- For dynamic libraries:
- You may need to construct an FFI-safe wrapper over `log`to initialize in your libraries

- You may need to construct an FFI-safe wrapper over
- Utilities:

[§](https://docs.rs#implementing-a-logger)Implementing a Logger

Loggers implement the [ Log](https://docs.rs/trait.Log.html) trait. Here’s a very basic example that simply
logs all messages at the

[,](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Error`[or](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Warn`[levels to stdout:](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Info````
use log::{Record, Level, Metadata};
struct SimpleLogger;
impl log::Log for SimpleLogger {
    fn enabled(&self, metadata: &Metadata) -> bool {
        metadata.level() <= Level::Info
    }
    fn log(&self, record: &Record) {
        if self.enabled(record.metadata()) {
            println!("{} - {}", record.level(), record.args());
        }
    }
    fn flush(&self) {}
}
```
Loggers are installed by calling the [ set_logger](https://docs.rs/fn.set_logger.html) function. The maximum
log level also needs to be adjusted via the

[function. The logging facade uses this as an optimization to improve performance of log messages at levels that are disabled. It’s important to set it, as it defaults to](https://docs.rs/fn.set_max_level.html)

`set_max_level`[, so no log messages will ever be captured! In the case of our example logger, we’ll want to set the maximum log level to](https://docs.rs/enum.LevelFilter.html)

`Off`[, since we ignore any](https://docs.rs/enum.LevelFilter.html)

`Info`[or](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Debug`[level log messages. A logging implementation should provide a function that wraps a call to](https://docs.rs/enum.Level.html)

`Trace`[and](https://docs.rs/fn.set_logger.html)

`set_logger`[, handling initialization of the logger:](https://docs.rs/fn.set_max_level.html)

`set_max_level````
use log::{SetLoggerError, LevelFilter};
static LOGGER: SimpleLogger = SimpleLogger;
pub fn init() -> Result<(), SetLoggerError> {
    log::set_logger(&LOGGER)
        .map(|()| log::set_max_level(LevelFilter::Info))
}
```
Implementations that adjust their configurations at runtime should take care to adjust the maximum log level as well.

[§](https://docs.rs#use-with-std)Use with `std`

`set_logger` requires you to provide a `&'static Log`, which can be hard to
obtain if your logger depends on some runtime configuration. The
`set_boxed_logger` function is available with the `std` Cargo feature. It is
identical to `set_logger` except that it takes a `Box<Log>` rather than a
`&'static Log`:

```
pub fn init() -> Result<(), SetLoggerError> {
    log::set_boxed_logger(Box::new(SimpleLogger))
        .map(|()| log::set_max_level(LevelFilter::Info))
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#compile-time-filters)Compile time filters

Log levels can be statically disabled at compile time by enabling one of these Cargo features:

- `max_level_off`
- `max_level_error`
- `max_level_warn`
- `max_level_info`
- `max_level_debug`
- `max_level_trace`

Log invocations at disabled levels will be skipped and will not even be present in the
resulting binary. These features control the value of the `STATIC_MAX_LEVEL` constant. The
logging macros check this value before logging a message. By default, no levels are disabled.

It is possible to override this level for release builds only with the following features:

- `release_max_level_off`
- `release_max_level_error`
- `release_max_level_warn`
- `release_max_level_info`
- `release_max_level_debug`
- `release_max_level_trace`

Libraries should avoid using the max level features because they’re global and can’t be changed once they’re set.

For example, a crate can disable trace level logs in debug builds and trace, debug, and info level logs in release builds with the following configuration:

```
[dependencies]
log = { version = "0.4", features = ["max_level_debug", "release_max_level_warn"] }
```
[§](https://docs.rs#crate-feature-flags)Crate Feature Flags

The following crate feature flags are available in addition to the filters. They are
configured in your `Cargo.toml`.

- `std`allows use of- `std`crate instead of the default- `core`. Enables using- `std::error`and- `set_boxed_logger`functionality.
- `serde`enables support for serialization and deserialization of- `Level`and- `LevelFilter`.

```
[dependencies]
log = { version = "0.4", features = ["std", "serde"] }
```
[§](https://docs.rs#version-compatibility)Version compatibility

The 0.3 and 0.4 versions of the `log` crate are almost entirely compatible. Log messages
made using `log` 0.3 will forward transparently to a logger implementation using `log` 0.4. Log
messages made using `log` 0.4 will forward to a logger implementation using `log` 0.3, but the
module path and file name information associated with the message will unfortunately be lost.

# myko - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/myko/^4.0.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#myko-rs---event-sourcing-cqrs-framework)Myko RS - Event-Sourcing CQRS Framework

`myko` is an actor-based event-sourcing framework for building real-time,
distributed systems with strong consistency guarantees.

[§](https://docs.rs#core-concepts)Core Concepts

| Concept | Description |
|---|---|
| Item | Base entity with typed `id` |
| Event | Immutable record of state change: `SET`(create/update) or`DEL`(delete) |
| Query | Request for live data stream, returns reactive `Observable<T[]>` |
| Report | Computed/derived data request, returns `Observable<T>` |
| Command | Intent to mutate state, returns result of operation |
| Saga | Stateful stream processor that reacts to events and emits commands |

[§](https://docs.rs#architecture)Architecture

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                             CellServer                                   │
│                                                                          │
│  WebSocket ──► WsHandler ──► CellServerCtx ──► StoreRegistry             │
│      │              │             │                   │                  │
│      │              │             │             CellMap<id, item>        │
│      │              ▼             │                   │                  │
│      │         Persister          │                   ▼                  │
│      │              │             │         Query/Report cells           │
│      │              ▼             │                   │                  │
│      │       Durable Backend ◄────────── Consumer                        │
│      │                                                                   │
│      ◄────────────────────── (subscription updates)                      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

Define an entity using the `#[myko_item]` attribute macro:

```
use myko::prelude::*;
#[myko_item]
pub struct Target {
    pub name: String,
    pub category: Option<String>,
    // id is added automatically
}
```
The macro auto-generates:

- `GetAllTargets`,- `GetTargetsByIds`,- `GetTargetsByQuery`queries
- `CountAllTargets`,- `CountTargets`,- `GetTargetById`reports
- `DeleteTarget`,- `DeleteTargets`commands
- `PartialTarget`struct for partial matching
- Registration with the `inventory`

[§](https://docs.rs#module-guide)Module Guide

| Module | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `client` | WebSocket client for connecting to Myko servers |
| `core` | Core types: command, query, report, saga, item, relationship |
| `wire` | Wire protocol types: MykoMessage, MEvent, responses, errors |
| `server` | CellServer and server context |
| `store` | Entity store and registry |

[§](https://docs.rs#performance)Performance

Myko-rs is optimized for high-throughput, low-latency scenarios:

- **Hyphae cells**: Reactive queries and reports using the hyphae cell library
- **Lock-free stores**: CellMap for concurrent entity access
- **MessagePack serialization**: Binary format for efficient WebSocket communication
- **Pluggable persistence**: Run in-memory for development, add Postgres for production persistence

See `libs/myko/rs/OPTIMIZATION.md` for detailed performance guidelines.

## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [myko_](https://docs.rs/attr.myko_command.html)- command

- [myko_](https://docs.rs/attr.myko_manual_cache_key.html)- manual_ - cache_ - key

- [myko_](https://docs.rs/attr.myko_subtype.html)- subtype

standard derives + serde camelCase rename + conditional TS export +
`register_ts_export!`so subtype definitions don’t repeat 3–4 lines of boilerplate each.
- [myko_](https://docs.rs/attr.myko_view.html)- view
- Defines a reactive view query.
- [myko_](https://docs.rs/attr.myko_view_item.html)- view_ - item

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

- [Partial](https://docs.rs/derive.PartialMatches.html)- Matches
- [TS](https://docs.rs/derive.TS.html)
- Noop replacement for `ts_rs::TS`derive — emits no trait impls and declares the`ts`helper attribute so user-written`#[ts(...)]`in entity source doesn’t error out when`ts_rs::TS`is absent.
- [TsNoop](https://docs.rs/derive.TsNoop.html)
- Noop replacement for `ts_rs::TS`derive — emits no trait impls and declares the`ts`helper attribute so user-written`#[ts(...)]`in entity source doesn’t error out when`ts_rs::TS`is absent.

# ts_rs - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ts-rs/^11.1/

## Expand description

#

ts-rs

Generate typescript type declarations from rust types

[§](https://docs.rs#why)Why?

When building a web application in rust, data structures have to be shared between backend and frontend. Using this library, you can easily generate TypeScript bindings to your rust structs & enums so that you can keep your types in one place.

ts-rs might also come in handy when working with webassembly.

[§](https://docs.rs#how)How?

ts-rs exposes a single trait, `TS`. Using a derive macro, you can implement this interface for your types.
Then, you can use this trait to obtain the TypeScript bindings.
We recommend doing this in your tests.
[See the example](https://github.com/Aleph-Alpha/ts-rs/blob/main/example/src/lib.rs) and [the docs](https://docs.rs/ts-rs/latest/ts_rs/).

[§](https://docs.rs#get-started)Get started

```
[dependencies]
ts-rs = "11.1"
```
```
use ts_rs::TS;
#[derive(TS)]
#[ts(export)]
struct User {
    user_id: i32,
    first_name: String,
    last_name: String,
}
```
When running `cargo test` or `cargo test export_bindings`, the TypeScript bindings will be exported to the file `bindings/User.ts`
and will contain the following code:

`export type User = { user_id: number, first_name: string, last_name: string, };`[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- generate type declarations from rust structs
- generate union declarations from rust enums
- inline types
- flatten structs/types
- generate necessary imports when exporting to multiple files
- serde compatibility
- generic types
- support for ESM imports

[§](https://docs.rs#cargo-features)cargo features

| Feature | Description |
|---|---|
| serde-compat | Enabled by defaultSee the “serde compatibility”section below for more information. |
| format | Enables formatting of the generated TypeScript bindings. Currently, this unfortunately adds quite a few dependencies. |
| no-serde-warnings | By default, warnings are printed during build if unsupported serde attributes are encountered. Enabling this feature silences these warnings. |
| serde-json-impl | Implement `TS`for types fromserde_json |
| chrono-impl | Implement `TS`for types fromchrono |
| bigdecimal-impl | Implement `TS`for types frombigdecimal |
| url-impl | Implement `TS`for types fromurl |
| uuid-impl | Implement `TS`for types fromuuid |
| bson-uuid-impl | Implement `TS`forbson::oid::ObjectIdandbson::uuid |
| bytes-impl | Implement `TS`for types frombytes |
| indexmap-impl | Implement `TS`for types fromindexmap |
| ordered-float-impl | Implement `TS`for types fromordered_float |
| heapless-impl | Implement `TS`for types fromheapless |
| semver-impl | Implement `TS`for types fromsemver |
| smol_str-impl | Implement `TS`for types fromsmol_str |
| tokio-impl | Implement `TS`for types fromtokio |

If there’s a type you’re dealing with which doesn’t implement `TS`, use either
`#[ts(as = "..")]` or `#[ts(type = "..")]`, or open a PR.

[§](https://docs.rs#serde-compatability)`serde` compatability

With the `serde-compat` feature (enabled by default), serde attributes can be parsed for enums and structs.
Supported serde attributes:

- `rename`
- `rename-all`
- `rename-all-fields`
- `tag`
- `content`
- `untagged`
- `skip`
- `skip_serializing`
- `skip_serializing_if`
- `flatten`
- `default`

Note: `skip_serializing` and `skip_serializing_if` only have an effect when used together with
`#[serde(default)]`.

Note: `skip_deserializing` is ignored. If you wish to exclude a field
from the generated type, but cannot use `#[serde(skip)]`, use `#[ts(skip)]` instead.

When ts-rs encounters an unsupported serde attribute, a warning is emitted, unless the feature `no-serde-warnings` is enabled.

[§](https://docs.rs#contributing)Contributing

Contributions are always welcome!
Feel free to open an issue, discuss using GitHub discussions or open a PR.
[See CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/Aleph-Alpha/ts-rs/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md)

[§](https://docs.rs#msrv)MSRV

The Minimum Supported Rust Version for this crate is 1.88.0

 Most of the time, you’d want to derive this trait instead of implementing it manually.
 ts-rs comes with implementations for all primitives, most collections, tuples, arrays and containers.

# parking_lot - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/parking_lot/^0.12/

## Expand description

This library provides implementations of `Mutex`, `RwLock`, `Condvar` and
`Once` that are smaller, faster and more flexible than those in the Rust
standard library. It also provides a `ReentrantMutex` type.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use ::`- [lock_api](https://docs.rs/lock_api/0.4.14/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/lock_api/index.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [deadlock](https://docs.rs/deadlock/index.html)
- [Experimental] Deadlock detection

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [ArcMutex](https://docs.rs/struct.ArcMutexGuard.html)- Guard
- An RAII mutex guard returned by the `Arc`locking operations on`Mutex`.
- [ArcReentrant](https://docs.rs/struct.ArcReentrantMutexGuard.html)- Mutex - Guard
- An RAII mutex guard returned by the `Arc`locking operations on`ReentrantMutex`.
- [ArcRw](https://docs.rs/struct.ArcRwLockReadGuard.html)- Lock - Read - Guard
- An RAII rwlock guard returned by the `Arc`locking operations on`RwLock`.
- [ArcRw](https://docs.rs/struct.ArcRwLockUpgradableReadGuard.html)- Lock - Upgradable - Read - Guard
- An RAII rwlock guard returned by the `Arc`locking operations on`RwLock`. This is similar to the`RwLockUpgradableReadGuard`struct, except instead of using a reference to unlock the`RwLock`it uses an`Arc<RwLock>`. This has several advantages, most notably that it has an`'static`lifetime.
- [ArcRw](https://docs.rs/struct.ArcRwLockWriteGuard.html)- Lock - Write - Guard
- An RAII rwlock guard returned by the `Arc`locking operations on`RwLock`. This is similar to the`RwLockWriteGuard`struct, except instead of using a reference to unlock the`RwLock`it uses an`Arc<RwLock>`. This has several advantages, most notably that it has an`'static`lifetime.
- [Condvar](https://docs.rs/struct.Condvar.html)
- A Condition Variable
- [Once](https://docs.rs/struct.Once.html)
- A synchronization primitive which can be used to run a one-time initialization. Useful for one-time initialization for globals, FFI or related functionality.
- [RawFair](https://docs.rs/struct.RawFairMutex.html)- Mutex
- Raw fair mutex type backed by the parking lot.
- [RawMutex](https://docs.rs/struct.RawMutex.html)
- Raw mutex type backed by the parking lot.
- [RawRw](https://docs.rs/struct.RawRwLock.html)- Lock
- Raw reader-writer lock type backed by the parking lot.
- [RawThread](https://docs.rs/struct.RawThreadId.html)- Id
- Implementation of the `GetThreadId`trait for`lock_api::ReentrantMutex`.
- [Wait](https://docs.rs/struct.WaitTimeoutResult.html)- Timeout - Result
- A type indicating whether a timed wait on a condition variable returned due to a time out or not.

- Current state of a `Once`.

- Creates a new fair mutex in an unlocked state ready for use.
- [const_](https://docs.rs/fn.const_mutex.html)- mutex
- Creates a new mutex in an unlocked state ready for use.

- Creates a new reentrant mutex in an unlocked state ready for use.

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- A mutual exclusion primitive useful for protecting shared data

- An RAII implementation of a “scoped lock” of a mutex. When this structure is dropped (falls out of scope), the lock will be unlocked.
- [Reentrant](https://docs.rs/type.ReentrantMutex.html)- Mutex
- A mutex which can be recursively locked by a single thread.

- RAII structure used to release the upgradable read access of a lock when dropped.
- [RwLock](https://docs.rs/type.RwLockWriteGuard.html)- Write - Guard
- RAII structure used to release the exclusive write access of a lock when dropped.
